title: [RFC]: Encoder-Only Prefill in P/D deployment for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash
body:
### Motivation.

## Summary

DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash can construct the target model's reusable global KV state without executing the complete decoder stack. In a P/D deployment where Decode already rebuilds sliding-window attention (SWA) state through bounded replay, this creates an opportunity to eliminate decoder computation on Prefill and initialize DSpark entirely on Decode.

This RFC proposes:

- P processes the **entire prompt** through the causal encoder L0–L19 and the minimal L20 path needed to produce the decoder's shared Main KV and Indexer K.
- P transfers the target's required global cache state. It does not produce or transfer target SWA or DSpark caches for this handoff.
- D uses the existing cache-hit-based bounded replay boundary, recomputes the tail through the complete target model, and samples the first output token.
- D derives DSpark context KV from the replay's target auxiliary hidden states, generates its own draft candidates, and continues with normal speculative decoding.

Unlike [RFC #57383](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/57383), this proposal does **not** reserve the last window of prompt tokens for first-time computation on D. P encodes all prompt positions, preserving the existing distinction between a cached replay window and an uncached suffix.

This is a design proposal, not an implemented or benchmarked optimization. “Encoder-only” includes the necessary boundary projections; it does not mean returning immediately after L19 without producing the decoder's global cache.

## Motivation

A conventional P worker retains the complete target model. When DSpark is enabled on P, the worker can also derive draft context KV and execute a proposal after target sampling. The example NIXL proxy forwards the original request and KV-transfer metadata to D, rather than forwarding P's sampled output and draft candidates as D's generation state.

When D subsequently performs bounded replay, it executes the target tail again and obtains the auxiliary features needed to initialize DSpark locally. Producing those features and draft caches on P is therefore avoidable if the handoff explicitly assigns their initialization to D.

The intended benefits are:

1. Remove target decoder attention/MoE computation from P, beyond the dependencies required to produce global cache state.
2. Allow P to omit decoder and DSpark weights in a later implementation phase.
3. Remove target SWA and draft cache transfers that D can rebuild.
4. Preserve the existing cache-hit-based replay model instead of introducing a new prompt-token ownership boundary.

The first implementation should prioritize correctness and a small execution change. Weight placement and GPU-count savings should be evaluated separately.

## Current Behavior and Code Baseline

The analysis below is based on vLLM commit [`41c4a3ed4e45792739bd8a5bbcd01269b06eae2c`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/tree/41c4a3ed4e45792739bd8a5bbcd01269b06eae2c), specifically the GPU Model Runner V2 and NIXL pull path. It is a source-level analysis, not an end-to-end validation of every P/D configuration.

- The [example NIXL proxy](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/41c4a3ed4e45792739bd8a5bbcd01269b06eae2c/tests/v1/kv_connector/nixl_integration/toy_proxy_server.py) asks P for one output token, extracts KV-transfer metadata, and sends the original request to D.
- The [runner](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/41c4a3ed4e45792739bd8a5bbcd01269b06eae2c/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py) invokes the configured speculator after sampling and before connector post-forward processing.
- [DSpark context precompute](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/41c4a3ed4e45792739bd8a5bbcd01269b06eae2c/vllm/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/dspark.py) projects target auxiliary features into each draft layer's window KV. The configured target layer IDs must retain their V4.1 attention-input semantics; they are not interchangeable with final normalized target output.
- [NIXL block exchange](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/41c4a3ed4e45792739bd8a5bbcd01269b06eae2c/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/base_scheduler.py) selects transferable groups and clips sliding-window groups to their tail blocks. It does not automatically omit a group merely because `prefix_cacheable=False`.
- The [scheduler](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/41c4a3ed4e45792739bd8a5bbcd01269b06eae2c/vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py) rewinds a loaded prefix by the replay window. [V4.1 model state](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/41c4a3ed4e45792739bd8a5bbcd01269b06eae2c/vllm/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/model_state.py) masks replay writes to prefix-cacheable groups while rebuilding SWA.

Consequently, removing P's decoder forward requires an explicit new handoff contract. It is not sufficient to skip layers while advertising their uninitialized caches as valid.

### Proposed Change.

### Model placement and execution

Use zero-based target layer numbering throughout.

| Component | P | D |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Embeddings and causal encoder L0–L19 | Run for all prompt positions, subject to existing valid prefix reuse | Run for replay and uncached suffix positions, then generated tokens |
| L20 global KV/Indexer producer path | Run for all positions requiring encoding | Preserve loaded entries during replay; produce new entries when appropriate |
| Remaining L20 computation and L21–L39 | Skip | Execute normally |
| Target SWA | Maintain encoder-local SWA needed for P computation; do not transfer it under this mode | Allocate and rebuild locally |
| Final normalization, LM head, output sampling | Not needed for this handoff | Generate the first output and subsequent outputs |
| DSpark auxiliary features and context KV | Do not produce | Produce from local target execution |
| DSpark proposals and target verification | Do not run | Run normally after initialization |

The L20 producer path must preserve every upstream operation needed for correct global cache bytes, including relevant mHC/normalization, projections, positional transforms, compression or packing, quantization metadata, and cache writes. It must not be approximated as an isolated linear projection.

P still needs its encoder SWA during encoding. “Do not transfer SWA” does not mean “do not compute encoder SWA.”

### Transfer contract

The new mode should explicitly identify the global cache groups produced by P and the locally reconstructed groups on D.

| State | Handoff policy |
| --- | --- |
| Required target global Main KV and Indexer cache state | Transfer, including the representation's required scales and metadata |
| Required boundary/compression continuation state | Preserve or reconstruct under an explicitly validated boundary rule |
| Target SWA | D-local reconstruction |
| DSpark context and query caches | D-local initialization |
| Target auxiliary hidden states | Not transferred |
| P output token, logits, draft IDs, draft probabilities | Not produced for handoff |
| Prompt, request configuration, cache coverage, transfer identity | Retained in the control path |

Declare a prefix available only after every required global group covers that prefix. A missing required global group remains a load failure. Missing SWA/draft state is expected under this mode and must not be mistaken for such a failure.

Do not infer the transfer set solely from `prefix_cacheable`. Use an explicit model-supported group selection, with matching layer identities, layouts, dtypes, quantization metadata, coverage, and TP/PP mapping on both sides.

### Replay boundary

Let:

- `N` be the prompt length;
- `H` be the actual prefix length adopted by D after connector limits and block alignment;
- `W` be the validated replay window, initially 128 for the supported configuration.

For an adopted hit with `H > W`:

```text
replay_start = H - W
cached replay positions = [H - W, H)
uncached suffix positions = [H, N)
D target positions to execute = [H - W, N)
```

Thus D processes `W + (N - H)` prompt positions in total, possibly across scheduler steps. It is exactly `W` only when `H == N`.

For hits too short to amortize replay, preserve the existing full-recompute behavior. For short prompts, D can run a cold prefill; bypassing P for such requests is an optional routing optimization, not a prerequisite.

During replay, preserve loaded global cache entries and prevent duplicate compression-state advancement. Newly computed suffix positions must still populate their required global caches. Block and compression boundaries remain authoritative.

### Request flow

1. The router sends P an explicit cache-production request for the full prompt.
2. P executes the encoder and required boundary producer path.
3. P reports cache readiness and transferable coverage after the relevant device work is complete. No actual generated token is required to complete this operation.
4. D receives the original request, allocates local state, and loads the declared global groups.
5. After load completion, D applies the existing cache-hit replay boundary.
6. D executes the target replay and any uncached suffix, rebuilding target SWA and exporting DSpark auxiliary features.
7. D samples the first output token when prompt processing completes.
8. D initializes DSpark context KV from valid target features before its first real proposal, then performs ordinary draft/verify iterations.

### Example

Assume a 1,024-token prompt, an adopted 1,024-token global-cache hit, a 128-token window, and three draft candidates per proposal.

| Step | Work |
| --- | --- |
| P | Encode positions `[0, 1024)` and produce required global caches; no decoder-tail forward or DSpark proposal |
| Transfer | Load global cache groups into D; do not load target SWA or draft groups |
| D replay | Execute target positions `[896, 1024)`, preserving loaded global entries and rebuilding local SWA |
| D sampling | Sample the first output `y0` from the final prompt position |
| D DSpark initialization | Combine local auxiliary features and write valid context KV for each draft layer |
| D proposal | Use `y0` as anchor to propose `d1, d2, d3` |
| D verification | Run target verification on `y0, d1, d2, d3`; retain accepted output and continue |

Rejected suffix rows must not become valid draft context. Existing rejection-aware context-slot handling should remain in effect.

### DSpark coverage requirement

D-local initialization is valid only if the locally recomputed target rows cover the context that the draft attention can read. Validate this against the draft model's actual attention window and position conventions; do not assume any arbitrary DSpark checkpoint fits a 128-token replay.

Initially, support only a known compatible V4.1 target/drafter pair. A wider-context or full-attention drafter requires a larger validated reconstruction scheme or a different handoff and is outside the initial scope.

Chunking must not expose uninitialized draft context. If the current speculator would run before enough replay context exists, add a request-local initialization guard or constrain initial admission/chunking. Final draft initialization must complete before a real proposal is used for verification.

## Implementation Scope

### Phase 1: Prove the execution and handoff contract

- Add an opt-in P execution mode that runs the global-cache producer path and skips decoder/output/draft work.
- Initially allow full target weight loading on P to keep weight-loader changes out of the first patch.
- Add an explicit cache-ready completion path instead of relying on `max_tokens=1` and real sampling. Propagate it through scheduler, runner, connector lifecycle, and router response handling.
- Restrict the transfer contract on both sides to required global state. Keep local D SWA/draft allocation independent from that transfer selection.
- Validate compatibility for the transferred target state even when P does not instantiate a DSpark speculator. Do not globally disable compatibility checking to permit asymmetric configurations.
- Reuse the existing replay machinery and local DSpark context precompute. Audit their initialization ordering, chunking, and write masks under this handoff.

### Phase 2: Reduce P memory residency

After correctness and performance are established, omit unused decoder, final-output, and DSpark weights on P. Preserve the original model architecture/configuration and explicitly select the execution/placement role; do not simulate this by changing the model's layer count.

Weight savings must be measured with embeddings, Engram placement, global caches, temporary buffers, CUDA graphs, and allocator headroom included. No specific single-GPU fit is claimed here.

### Initial support boundary

Start with text-only requests, NIXL pull, GPU Model Runner V2, PP=1, no prefill context parallelism or microbatching, and a fixed supported DSpark configuration. Require the replay feature to be active; fail clearly or use the complete conventional path when it is unavailable.

Prompt-logprob requests require a separate fallback because their requested outputs cannot generally be produced by an encoder-only P path and a short D replay. Extend parallelism and connector support after the initial contract is validated.

## Relationship to RFC #57383

| Aspect | RFC #57383 | This proposal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| P prompt range | Prefix `[0, N-W)` | Entire prompt `[0, N)` |
| P model path | Encoder plus necessary boundary projection | Same intended producer path |
| D first target range | Intended final window `[N-W, N)` | `[H-W, N)`, based on adopted cache coverage |
| Tail global KV | First produced by D | Already produced by P where transferred; preserved during replay |
| DSpark initialization | Needs explicit integration | Explicitly assigned to D |
| Scheduler semantics | Requires coordinating reserved-tail execution with replay | Preserves hit-based replay semantics |
| Extra P work | Avoids encoding the reserved tail | Encodes that tail as well |

If `H=N-W`, applying today's additional `W`-token rewind would start D at `N-2W`. This proposal avoids that particular mismatch by keeping full-prompt encoding and interpreting D work through the actual cache hit.

The trade-off is deliberate: retain a bounded amount of duplicate encoder work to reduce the initial change in scheduling and cache-boundary semantics. This is not a claim that every component of this RFC is already supported.

## Expected Benefits and Costs

The computation benefit depends on the baseline. Against full-prompt execution through the complete target, removing decoder work can be substantial. Against an implementation that already restricts decoder work to a trailing window, the removed work is only that decoder tail plus P-side DSpark/output work.

D still pays target replay and context-KV projection costs. If the baseline already performs the same replay, this proposal does not inherently add another replay. Any extra cost from changed draft initialization or scheduling must be measured.

Potential benefits include lower P latency, fewer P MoE/collective operations, less cache-transfer traffic, and eventually lower P weight residency. Potential costs include D admission bursts, non-uniform batches or CUDA-graph fallback, and transfer-contract complexity.

Bounded replay is not bit-equivalent to a cold full prefill. The primary comparison should therefore be against the same replay-enabled P/D baseline; a cold/full-state path remains a secondary quality reference.

## Validation Plan

1. **Producer correctness:** compare required global cache contents and coverage with the conventional P path under identical numerical settings, including quantization scales and boundary state.
2. **Transfer correctness:** confirm that no SWA/draft groups are advertised or loaded in this mode, while every required global group is covered. Exercise block-aligned and unaligned prompt lengths.
3. **Replay correctness:** verify global-write masking, suffix writes, SWA reconstruction, short hits, load failure, cancellation, and preemption recovery.
4. **DSpark initialization:** verify auxiliary-feature selection, context coverage, initialization ordering, accepted/rejected rows, and no reads from uninitialized draft positions. Compare draft acceptance and quality against the replay-enabled baseline.
5. **Performance:** measure P latency and throughput, end-to-end TTFT, D P50/P95/P99 ITL, transferred bytes by group, draft acceptance length, and P/D memory residency. Sweep prompt length, arrival rate, and concurrent decodes.

A successful implementation must demonstrate valid state ownership and no quality regression beyond the chosen replay baseline before claims about replica sizing or throughput gains.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Keep full P execution and transfer DSpark KV:** smallest execution change when the existing symmetric path works, but retains deep target computation and weights on P. D replay may update the same draft context again.
- **Transfer target auxiliary hidden states:** still requires deep target execution on P and introduces an activation handoff; it does not achieve the main P-side savings.
- **Implement RFC #57383 directly:** potentially avoids the duplicate encoder tail, but adds reserved-tail and replay-boundary integration to the first implementation.
- **Transfer all SWA state and avoid replay:** a different latency/bandwidth trade-off that retains the P decoder state-production dependency.

## Open Questions / Feedback Requested

- What is the smallest reusable interface for cache-only request completion without a generated token?
- Should transferable-group selection be expressed as a model-specific handoff profile or a broader connector capability?
- How should compatibility checks admit P-without-DSpark while preserving strict validation of transferred target state?
- Which existing DSpark initialization guards are sufficient for chunked replay, and which need extension?
- Can weight omission be isolated from the initial execution patch without retaining unwanted cache allocations?

## Status and Ownership

Draft proposal. No implementation, benchmark results, or implementation ownership is asserted. This RFC is intended to solicit feedback on the execution boundary, cache-transfer contract, and DSpark initialization requirements.

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

_No response_

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: FlashInfer autotune for trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe wedges forever on SM103 (GB300): trtllm_gemm cubin is sm_100a-only, no PTX, and the autotuner has no timeout
body:
> **EDIT (2026-09-23):** The root-cause attribution below is **withdrawn**. `nm -D` shows the `fp4_block_scale_moe` symbols live in `fused_moe_trtllm_sm100.so` (which carries `sm_103a` cubins), not `trtllm_gemm.so` (the dense GEMM module — the sm_100a-only observation is real but irrelevant to this op). The "candidate can never execute on SM103" mechanism does not hold. The symptom stands (unbounded autotune at boot, 40+ min, zero progress lines, no cache write before termination); it is now considered a probable extreme-slow-crawl rather than a proven hang, since the autotuner logs nothing between start and end and only writes the cache on completion. See [this comment](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/58031#issuecomment-5788562400) for the corrected analysis and proposed scoping (exclude SM103 from `FLASHINFER_TRTLLM_MXFP4_MXFP8` auto-selection; add per-bucket progress logging). The workaround below remains valid.

## Describe the bug

On a DGX Station GB300 (SM103, compute capability 10.3), the FlashInfer autotune for `trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe` runs indefinitely at 100% GPU with zero progress and zero autotune cache writes, wedging engine startup forever. There is no error, no traceback, no timeout — the boot simply never completes.

The root cause appears to be an arch-coverage gap in FlashInfer's prebuilt `trtllm_gemm` cubin, combined with an autotuner that has no timeout for a candidate kernel that never terminates.

## Environment

- Image: `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly` pulled 2026-09-21 (vLLM `0.29.1rc1.dev452+g3df4ae153`, FlashInfer `0.6.18.post1`), arm64
- GPU: NVIDIA GB300 (SM103), driver 610.43.02
- Model: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (MXFP4 experts / MXFP8 rest), TP1, `--cpu-offload-gb 75`, DSpark speculative k=5
- Flags relevant: `--max-num-batched-tokens 16384`, moe backend auto-selects `FLASHINFER_TRTLLM_MXFP4_MXFP8`

## Reproduction

Serve DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (or any model that routes MoE through `trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe`) on SM103 **without** skipping the op's autotune. Boot proceeds normally through weight load, CUDA graph capture, and JIT warmup, then reaches:

```
[flashinfer_sparse_mla_warmup.py:267] Warming up DeepSeek V4 sparse MLA attention for mixed tokens=16.
[kernel_warmup.py:436] Using FlashInfer autotune cache file: .../autotune_configs.json
autotuner.py:972 - flashinfer.jit: [Autotuner]: Autotuning process starts ...
[kernel_warmup.py:358] Running FlashInfer autotune with 16384 tokens and token buckets (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 768, 1024, 1280, 1536, 1792, 2048, 2560, 3072, 3584, 4096, 8192, 16384).
```

… and stays there. Observed: 40+ minutes at 100% GPU utilization, 0 new log lines in any 10-minute window, and the cache directory for the config hash created but left **empty**:

```
drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Sep 21 15:35 .   # created when autotune started
# (no autotune_configs.json ever written)
```

By contrast, the JIT kernel warmup immediately before it completes with per-batch progress lines (10/10 batches in 47s), so the wedge is specific to this op's autotune, not to warmup in general.

The same behavior existed on the launch-day `deepseekv41-flash-0909` image, which is why this deployment has carried `VLLM_FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNE_SKIP_OPS="trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe,flashinfer::trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe"` since September 9. Reproducing it on current nightly shows the gap is not fixed.

## Root cause evidence

Inspecting FlashInfer's prebuilt cubins in the nightly image (`flashinfer_jit_cache`):

```console
# 907 .so files in flashinfer_jit_cache overall — sm_103a coverage exists:
$ for so in $(find . -name "*.so"); do cuobjdump -lelf $so 2>/dev/null | grep -oE "sm_103[a-z]?"; done | sort | uniq -c
   3380 sm_103a

# …but the cubin the fp4 block-scale MoE autotuner benchmarks:
$ cuobjdump -lelf .../jit_cache/trtllm_gemm/trtllm_gemm.so | grep -oE "sm_[0-9]+[a-z]?" | sort | uniq -c
      1 sm_100a

$ cuobjdump -ptx .../jit_cache/trtllm_gemm/trtllm_gemm.so | grep -oE "target sm_[0-9]+" | sort | uniq -c
      (empty — no PTX section at all)
```

`trtllm_gemm.so` ships **only an `sm_100a` cubin and no PTX**. An arch-specific (`a`-suffixed) cubin runs on exactly its target arch and never on a later one (this is the same mechanism as the `cooperative_topk` SM103 gap documented in the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash SM103 patch work — `sm_100a` cubins are unusable on SM103, and without PTX there is nothing to JIT forward).

So on SM103 the autotuner launches a candidate that either fails its launch silently or spins in a grid-stride loop sized for a different arch, and the `cudaEventSynchronize` in the timing loop blocks forever. The autotuner has no per-candidate timeout, so one non-terminating candidate wedges the whole boot.

## Suggested fixes (either would do; both would be robust)

1. **Ship an `sm_103a` (and ideally `sm_103`-JITable PTX) build of `trtllm_gemm`** — the rest of the JIT cache clearly builds for 103a (3,380 cubins), so this specific module looks like an omission rather than a fundamental limitation.
2. **Add a timeout to the FlashInfer autotuner per candidate/bucket** — a wedged candidate should be skipped and logged, not hang the engine forever. Right now one bad kernel costs an unbounded boot.

## Workaround

```
VLLM_FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNE_SKIP_OPS="trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe,flashinfer::trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe"
```

With the skip, the same configuration boots to serving in ~8 minutes; the op then runs on its default (untuned) kernel selection. Measured decode on this deployment is ~91 tok/s single-stream with the skip in place.

## Additional context

- Full deployment config and the SM103 patch history: https://github.com/ebfio/deepseek-v4.1-flash-gb300
- The engine does not log *which* candidate config it was benchmarking when it wedged — if maintainers want a `py-spy dump` from a wedged process or a CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING run, I can reproduce the wedge on demand and capture it.

title: [Bug]: OpenAI-compatible Embeddings API intermittently crashes with multimodal cache assertion (`Expected a cached item for mm_hash`) on Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Using vLLM `serve` with the OpenAI-compatible **Embeddings API** to run **Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B**, the server intermittently crashes while pre-processing embedding requests. The crash is an assertion inside the multimodal feature cache:

```
AssertionError: Expected a cached item for mm_hash='...'
```

After that, the API server hits a second assertion:

```
AssertionError: assert req_state.detokenizer is not None
```

This suggests the request fails during `preprocess_add_request()` when the engine tries to retrieve multimodal features from `mm_receiver_cache`, but the cache entry for the computed `mm_hash` is missing; then the output handler processes an incomplete request state.

## Environment / deployment

- API: OpenAI-compatible **Embeddings** endpoint
- Deployment: cloud vendor managed model inference service (default settings; limited ability to tune internal worker settings)
- Model: `Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B`
- Launch command:

```bash
vllm serve /mnt/data \
  --runner pooling \
  --dtype bfloat16 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 2 \
  --max-model-len 65536 \
  --trust-remote-code
```

## Steps to reproduce

This occurs intermittently under real traffic. We don’t have a 100% minimal repro yet, but it happens when sending embedding requests with multimodal inputs to the OpenAI-compatible embeddings endpoint.

## Observed behavior (logs)

```text
(EngineCore_DP0 pid=151) ERROR ... Unexpected error pre-processing request ...
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../vllm/v1/engine/core.py", line 1142, in process_input_sockets
    request = self.preprocess_add_request(req)
  File ".../vllm/v1/engine/core.py", line 621, in preprocess_add_request
    request.mm_features = self.mm_receiver_cache.get_and_update_features(...)
  File ".../vllm/multimodal/cache.py", line 594, in get_and_update_features
    feature.data = self.get_and_update_item(feature.data, cache_key)
  File ".../vllm/multimodal/cache.py", line 647, in get_and_update_item
    assert mm_item is not None, f"Expected a cached item for {mm_hash=}"
AssertionError: Expected a cached item for mm_hash='1bdd9fe1df7949177eff89badb62b8d7904c75ea8d60d6826388faa1f105531d'

(APIServer pid=30) ERROR ... AsyncLLM output_handler failed.
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py", line 664, in output_handler
    processed_outputs = output_processor.process_outputs(...)
  File ".../vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py", line 629, in process_outputs
    assert req_state.detokenizer is not None
AssertionError
```

## Expected behavior

- The embeddings request should either succeed, or fail gracefully with a clear error response.
- vLLM should not `assert` and crash due to a missing multimodal cache item; if the cache misses, it should recompute the multimodal features or safely reject the request and clean up request state so the output handler does not assert.

## Additional notes / hypotheses

- Since we are using a cloud vendor inference service, the internal runtime might use multiple processes/workers or request routing patterns that could make multimodal caches non-sticky across workers.
- The error strongly looks like a multimodal cache inconsistency / race / eviction, or cross-process cache visibility issue: the engine expects a cached `mm_hash` item but cannot find it.

Thanks!

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [Feature]: Process-level PD Disaggregation within Single Instance
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

### Description of the Feature Proposal
This proposal outlines a new scheduling and execution mechanism called "Process-level PD Disaggregation". The core idea is to spatially partition a single GPU's resources to run compute-bound prefill operations and memory-bound decode operations concurrently.

This is achieved by launching separate processes for prefill and decode on the same GPU, managed by NVIDIA MPS  and multiple stream. This approach enables resource sharing between the two distinct workloads, improving overall GPU utilization and allowing the system to meet strict SLOs for both TTFT and ITL.

### Motivation for the Proposal
LLM serving in production environments faces a critical challenge: simultaneously optimizing for TTFT and ITL. During traffic surges, single-instance deployments struggle to balance these two metrics, making it difficult to meet strict SLOs, such as TTFT < 1.3s and avg. ITL < 30ms. 

The prefill stage is typically compute-bound, while the decode stage is memory-bound, leading to inefficient use of GPU resources when these operations are scheduled sequentially. A promising approach is to overlap these two phases to maximize resource utilization. This feature aims to implement such an overlapping mechanism to solve the trade-off between TTFT and ITL.

### Specific Problem
I'm working on serving a Qwen2-32B model under high, concurrent traffic and need to maintain a high-quality user experience defined by strict SLOs.

Current strategies, such as chunked prefill, are insufficient. Chunked prefill breaks a large prefill request into smaller chunks and batches them with decode requests. While this method effectively reduces ITL and improves GPU utilization compared to a prefill-priority policy, it introduces a severe regression in TTFT.

To validate this in our production environment (average output length of 4K, average input length of 12K), we tested the impact of different chunk sizes. Our findings show a direct and problematic trade-off: smaller chunk sizes lower ITL but dramatically increase TTFT. This is because each subsequent chunk must re-access the KV cache generated by previous chunks, introducing significant memory access and scheduling overhead.

The data below illustrates this problem. As we decrease the chunk size , P99+ ITL improves, but average TTFT increases beyond our SLO of 1.3s.

| Chunk Size |  3K | 4K | 5K | No-Chunk |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Average TTFT (ms) | 1445 | 1394 | 1299 | 1108.32 |
| Average ITL (ms) | 21 | 20 | 19 | 20.43 |
| P99 ITL (ms) | 227 | 274 | 297 | 400.31 |
| P99.2 ITL (ms) | 235 | 288 | 309 | 515.07 |
| P99.4 ITL (ms) | 242 | 302 | 329 | 675.18 |
| P99.6 ITL (ms) | 249 | 319 | 351 | 882.51 |
| P99.8 ITL (ms) | 262 | 336 | 374 | 1179.15 |
| Max ITL (ms) | 883 | 1036 | 1051 | 3950 |
| Requests with ITL > 400ms (%) | 4% | 39.40% | 72% | 82% |
| Stutters per Request | 1 | 1.29 | 2.22 | 3.85 |
| Stutter Rate (%) | 3.760% | 5.700% | 23.000% | 81.000% |
| Position of First Stutter | 204 | 269 | 228 | 92 |


### Resource Utilization in LLM
To understand the root cause, we profiled the SM utilization of different operations during the prefill stage on a vLLM 0.9.1 deployment (Qwen2-32B, 8 x H20). The results confirm that prefill is a compute-bound phase, with many kernels achieving high SM utilization. In contrast, the decode phase is memory-bound and exhibits consistently low SM utilization.

Prefill Stage SM Utilization (%) for Various Operations:
Operations | Kernel | 1k | 2k | 4k | 8k | 16k | 32k
-- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | --
Input RMS | fused_add_rms | 33.0 | 67.0 | 84.5 | 80.3 | 95.4 | 95.4
QKV | nvje | 88.3 | 89.2 | 97.1 | 93.8 | 99.3 | 95.8
Rotation Embedding | rotation_embeding | 92.0 | 73.0 | 90.0 | 85.0 | 93.0 | 91.7
Attention | reshape_and_cache | 92.0 | 73.0 | 90.0 | 85.0 | 93.0 | 96.0
  | fa_fwd | 78.1 | 71.0 | 70.3 | 86.4 | 89.3 | 99.0
  | fa_fwd_combine | 70.0 | 66.0 | 76.0 | 57.0 | 40.0 | 100.0
Row Parallel Linear | nvjet | 70.0 | 66.3 | 82.2 | 88.5 | 71.5 | 93.2
  | nccl | 35.5 | 33.3 | 30.7 | 28.1 | 23.2 | 21.9
Output RMS | fused_add_rms | 55.3 | 35.4 | 71.3 | 80.5 | 88.0 | 96.5
MLP | nvje | 91.5 | 94.7 | 98.0 | 98.9 | 98.8 | 99.6
  | silu | 92.4 | 82.0 | 87.6 | 87.3 | 97.2 | 99.2
  | nvtj | 92.8 | 94.8 | 96.4 | 98.2 | 96.9 | 95.8
  | nccl | 34.3 | 44.9 | 26.2 | 24.9 | 22.2 | 46.8

The low utilization during communication  and the memory-bound nature of decode create a significant opportunity for optimization. By allowing prefill and decode to share GPU resources spatially, we can service high-priority decode requests while backfilling the GPU with compute-intensive prefill work.

### Proposed Solution
Inspired by concepts from works like Semi-PD, we propose implementing intra-instance prefill/decode disaggregation. This involves the following core features:

1. Multi-Process Architecture: For each GPU, we will launch two independent processes: one for Prefill and one for Decode. NVIDIA MPS will be used to enable spatial sharing of the GPU hardware, allowing kernels from both processes to execute concurrently.
2. Multi-Stream Execution: The Prefill and Decode processes will be mapped to separate CUDA streams. This allows the hardware to overlap operations.
3. Unified Cross-Process Memory Management: A unified memory manager will be created to handle the KV cache. This manager will use CUDA IPC to share GPU memory handles between the Prefill and Decode processes, ensuring the Decode process can seamlessly read the KV cache generated by the Prefill process.
4. SM Controller: It will dynamically modify the SM mask in the Thread Management Descriptor to control which kernels execute on which TPCs.
5. SLO-Aware Scheduler: The central scheduler will be enhanced to: 1) Route incoming requests to the Prefill and Decode processes. 2)Use an integrated simulator to predict the execution time of prefill and decode tasks. 3) Dynamically adjust the SM resource allocation based on current load and SLO targets.
6. Layer-wise Chunked Prefill: To avoid the high overhead of token-level chunking, prefill computation will be chunked at the layer level. This allows a long prefill to be paused and resumed between layers, creating opportunities for the scheduler to execute high-priority decode batches. A brief sleep or yield mechanism will be added to the prefill loop to ensure the Decode process can preemptively seize resources during contention.


Our proposed approach has been preliminarily implemented and validated on the sglang, where it has already demonstrated promising performance gains in balancing TTFT and ITL under our workload. This work is further detailed in our paper, "Boosting LLM Serving through Spatial-Temporal GPU Resource Sharing" and the proof-of-concept implementation is available at: https://github.com/zejia-lin/BulletServe.

We are currently in the process of refactoring and hardening the system for production use. We believe this “Process-level Prefill/Decode Disaggregation within a Single Instance” feature would be a valuable addition to vLLM. We are keen to collaborate with the community to integrate this functionality, enhancing vLLM's capabilities for serving mission-critical, low-latency LLM applications.

title: [RFC]: Asymmetric P/D Deployment for DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash
body:
## Summary. DeepSeek-V4.1's bounded-replay structure creates an opportunity to make Prefill/Decode disaggregation substantially more asymmetric. Today, a Prefill worker still loads the full 40-layer model even though, after layer 20, only the final 128 prompt tokens need to be processed. This keeps almost half of the model weights resident on P for a small decoder-layer workload whose MoE utilization is likely poor. This RFC proposes moving that final 128-token window entirely to the Decode worker: - For a prompt of length `N`, P computes only `[0, N-128)` and transfers the resulting prefix KV state. - D computes `[N-128, N)` as its first full-model step and samples the first output token. - The request then continues through normal speculative decode with `q_len = 1 + num_spec_tokens`. This asymmetry has two main benefits. - First, P would load only the causal encoder plus the minimal layer-20 KV/Indexer projection path, potentially removing close to half of its transformer-layer weights; a key target is fitting a production Prefill replica on one B300 GPU. - Second, moving the decoder-layer work to D increases the computational intensity of that work by executing it as part of D's much larger token batches, improving utilization relative to processing the 128-token replay on P. The execution model on D also becomes simpler than layer-local decoder replay. D never needs separate encoder and decoder token batches: ```text first D step: all L0-L39 process the same 128 prompt tokens later D steps: all L0-L39 process the same 1 + num_spec_tokens tokens ``` The trade-off is that each newly admitted request contributes 128 bounded-prefill tokens to a D step, which can temporarily increase the Decode token count and affect ITL (TPOT). This incremental cost is expected to be modest for DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash: its light KV cache permits large Decode batches, and DSpark also makes each Decode batch process many tokens. Against that baseline, adding 128 tokens when a new request is admitted is a relatively small increase. This RFC is a design proposal for discussion. I do not currently plan to implement it, and there is no prototype or benchmark result yet. Implementation ownership is open. ## Proposed Change. ### Model placement and token ownership ```mermaid flowchart LR I[Prompt: N tokens] I -->|Prefix: N-W tokens| P I -->|Final window: W tokens| D subgraph P[Prefill worker: partial model] PE[Causal encoder L0-L19] PK[Minimal L20 Main-KV / Indexer
projection path] PE --> PK end subgraph D[Decode worker: full model] BR[First step: bounded prefill
L0-L39, q_len = W] FT[Sample first output token] ND[Later steps: speculative decode
L0-L39, q_len = 1 + num_spec_tokens] BR --> FT --> ND end P -->|Prefix Main / Indexer KV| D ``` For prompts no longer than `W`, P performs no model forward and D processes the complete prompt. Conceptually, P would retain: - embeddings and complete layers L0-L19; - the minimal layer-20 projections needed to produce its canonical C1 Main KV and Indexer K; and - the state required by the KV connector handoff. P would not retain the complete layer-20 attention/MoE path, layers 21–39, final normalization, or the LM head. ### Request flow ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant P as Prefill worker participant D as Decode worker P->>P: Run prompt prefix [0, N-W) P->>P: Produce prefix Main/Indexer KV P->>D: Send prefix KV D->>D: First step: run final W prompt tokens D->>D: Sample first output token D->>D: Later steps: normal speculative decode ``` Moving first-token generation to Decode is intentional. To minimize changes to the P-node scheduler, the P-node can compute the entire prompt (N tokens) instead of (N−W) tokens, since W is generally much smaller than N and the resulting redundant computation is negligible. ### Uniform Decode execution Decode has two full-model step shapes: ```text new request, first step: q_len = W active layers = L0-L39 later speculative decode steps: q_len = 1 + num_spec_tokens active layers = L0-L39 ``` The first step is a bounded prefill using the transferred prefix state. After sampling, the request joins normal speculative decoding. This avoids changing the token set after layer 20. The attention history differs by cache group, but the query rows do not: - prefix-cacheable Main/Indexer groups read the transferred prefix state; - SWA groups are rebuilt locally over the replay window, following the mechanism in #56227; and - every layer executes the same `W` query rows in the first D step. If bounded-prefill requests and ongoing decode requests are scheduled together, their request-level `q_len` values differ. This step is a non-uniform batch and may fallback to piecewise cudagraph. ## Why This May Help. ### Smaller Prefill replicas Prefill node no longer needs the complete decoder stack or LM head. This is expected to remove close to **`half of the weights`** from each Prefill node. The exact saving depends on embeddings, KV pools, connector buffers, CUDA graphs, and allocator headroom. For DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash, savings map straight to GPUs: tiny KV cache + offloading make Prefill HBM weight-bound, so halving transformer weights nearly halves the Prefill GPU count. A key target is fitting one production Prefill replica on a single B300 GPU. ### Avoid a low-density late-decoder tail on P The bounded replay contains at most 128 tokens per new request. Running it on P produces a small decoder-layer token workload and low arithmetic intensity because Prefill batchsize is usually small. In this proposal, D executes the final window as an ordinary full-model bounded-prefill step. It can batch multiple newly admitted requests and coordinate them with the larger Decode workload to get a **`higher arithmetic intensity`**. ### Simpler, unified model execution The split is by workers and token ranges, not by layer ranges within a forward: - P runs the entire model (encoder + layer-20 KV/Indexer projection path) on the prompt, using the same workload throughout each step—no workload reset between encoder and decoder layers. - D runs the entire model (encoder + decoder) on the bounded final window or normal decode workload. This makes the execution architecture **`simpler and more uniform`**, while naturally accommodating Chunked Prefill, Prefix Caching, and Context Parallelism. ### Cost and Trade-offs. The main cost is a larger first step on D: ```text new request, first step: q_len <= 128 later steps: q_len = 1 + num_spec_tokens ``` Potential costs include: - D must support both bounded-prefill and speculative-decode shapes. - Admission bursts may increase ITL/TPOT for running requests. - Mixing both request types in one scheduler iteration may require piecewise CUDA graphs or eager fallback. This is likely **`acceptable`** for DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash because its compressed KV cache permits a **`large Decode batch`**, and steps admitting new requests are usually a small fraction of all Decode steps. This requires measurement. ## Relationship to Existing vLLM Work. This proposal builds on, but is different from, two open vLLM PRs. ### #56227: encoder-side SWA bounded replay [#56227](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56227) already provides much of the required runtime behavior: - after a local or KV-connector prefix hit ending at `H`, the scheduler rewinds the final window; - the worker recomputes `[H-W, H)` locally; - Main/Indexer KV remains cached or transferred, while SWA is rebuilt locally; and - `Request.replay_start` and attention metadata floor the replay window. This PR is nearly orthogonal to the current RFC and provides sound logic for the P node's execution. ### #56752: decoder-side SWA bounded replay [#56752](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56752) compacts the batch after layer 20 so layers 21–39 process only each request's trailing window. That design still performs one forward in which different layer ranges process different token sets: ```text L0-L20: full prompt rows L21-L39: trailing W rows ``` This RFC proposes a different deployment boundary: ```text P: [0, N-W), L0-L19 and L20's KV/Indexer projection path D: [N-W, N), through all L0-L39 ``` Within a Decode step, every layer processes the same rows. There is no layer-20 compaction boundary, internal gather/scatter, or replay-layer sub-batch. ### Feedback Period. ### CC List. _No response_ ### Any Other Things. _No response_ ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [Performance]: 【求助】8卡H200跑DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash，并发才8就慢成狗，首字等好几分钟，有没有大佬遇到过？
body:
### Proposal to improve performance

机器是8张H200，2T内存，本地NVMe放的模型。vLLM用的nightly镜像，部署的DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash。

报错那次完整的启动命令如下：

sudo docker run -d
--name deepseek-v41-flash
--gpus all
--privileged
--ipc=host
--shm-size=128g
-p 30003:30003
-v /data/3/lyp/models/deepseek_v4_1_flash/:/models/deepseek_v4_1_flash
-e VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S=3600
-e HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1
-e VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1
vllm/vllm-openai:nightly /models/deepseek_v4_1_flash
--tokenizer-mode deepseek_v41
--enable-expert-parallel
--tensor-parallel-size 8
--tool-call-parser deepseek_v41
--enable-auto-tool-choice
--reasoning-parser deepseek_v41
--trust-remote-code
--no-enable-flashinfer-autotune
--gpu-memory-utilization 0.90
--max-model-len 1048576
--max-num-seqs 64
--enable-prefix-caching
--port 30003
--speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":5,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic","rejection_sample_method":"block","enable_adaptive_verification":true}'
--mm-encoder-tp-mode data
--kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"SimpleCPUOffloadConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_extra_config":{"cpu_bytes_to_use_per_rank":171798691840,"lazy_offload":true}}'

后来去掉--kv-transfer-config也试过，一样慢。

现在问题是：并发才8个请求，就卡得不行。New API那边看日志全是“首字不适用”，frt=-1000，就是vLLM压根没吐第一个token出来。等个2到15分钟，客户端直接超时断了，completion_tokens=0。

vLLM自己的日志里 Reqs Running: 8，但 Avg generation tput: 0.0 toks/s，GPU KV cache used 才1%左右。Prefix cache hit rate也是抽风，一会98%一会0%。

nvidia-smi看，SM跑满100%，但mem才6%到28%，PCIe接收倒是有2.5到7 GB/s。GPU温度功耗都正常，ECC也全是0。之前有张卡报过Xid 95，重置后没再犯。

请求的prompt都巨长，几万到几十万token，reasoning_effort基本都是high或max。我怀疑是超长上下文把prefill队列堵死了，decode根本排不上，所以generation tput才是0。也可能Engram表放CPU内存，PCIe来回搬数据太慢。

试过去掉KV offload，没用。Rust前端启动时还提示有些参数不生效。CUDA Graph捕获的时候一堆空图警告，但最后显示都100%完成了。

有没有人遇到过类似情况？是不是必须把max-model-len降下来？或者换回Python前端？还是说Engram这块目前就是坑？求指点，感谢！

title: [RFC]: Increase vLLM Review Capacity with a Reviewer Role
body:
## Motivation

vLLM’s contribution volume exceeds its available review and triage capacity, creating a massive PR backlog. To help address this backlog and stem its future growth, we propose a **Reviewer** role to expand the community of trusted reviewers who take ownership of triage and initial review, helping authors bring their PRs up to vLLM’s standards. Today, much of that responsibility falls on committers, who must balance review with implementation, architectural decisions, releases, and maintenance.

The growing volume of low-quality AI-generated contributions (“AI slop”) compounds this problem, increasing the effort required to identify worthwhile changes and bring them up to project standards. The Reviewer title also recognizes review as a valuable contribution and establishes a clearer path toward committership.

## The Reviewer Role

Reviewers take ownership of triage and initial review, helping contributors bring their PRs up to vLLM’s standards. This includes understanding the problem, evaluating the proposed solution, examining correctness and validation, and working with authors to resolve concerns. Reviewers help address common issues that consume review capacity, including unnecessary complexity, poorly scoped changes, overspecified tests, unjustified modifications to core code, and missing performance measurements or accuracy evaluations. Addressing these issues is especially valuable as AI-generated contributions increase.

Reviewer status formally recognizes contributors’ review work and the trust they have earned within the project. Following [Kubernetes’ reviewer/approver model](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/b8ce3416617273bfb8611b18b4cd8412893e44db/community-membership.md), authors are expected to address reviewer feedback by making changes or responding with an explanation before requesting final committer review. Outstanding concerns must be resolved, or explicitly adjudicated by a committer, before the PR is merged. Reviewers should involve relevant committers when questions require their input.

The formal title signals to contributors that reviewer feedback is part of the project’s acceptance process and must be addressed. It also signals to other committers that they can rely on reviewers’ judgment within the scope of the review they performed.

Reviewers can:

- Review PRs and provide a recognized approval or request changes.  
- Trigger CI when a contribution is ready for evaluation.  
- Escalate design questions to the appropriate committer and SIG.  
- Triage PRs/issues and apply appropriate labels; flagging potentially important PRs that should receive expedited committer attention.  
- Close duplicate PRs/issues to cut down noise and focus effort on the most promising contributions.  
- Flag PRs that are ready for committer review, approval, and merge.

Reviewers cannot:

- Merge PRs into main themselves, even when approved and CI is green.

A completed reviewer pass should give the committer a useful starting point: what was checked, what evidence is available, and what still needs committer attention. Ideally, committer review should be minimal at this point, mostly an LGTM and final approval, with substantive concerns already addressed during reviewer-led triage and initial review.

Substantive requests for changes must be resolved before merge, either through revisions or an explicit resolution by a committer. Authors may ask for clarification or escalate disagreements; reviewer status does not make every preference a requirement. Reviewer approval signals readiness for final consideration. It does not replace committer review or guarantee acceptance.

## Assigning Reviewers

A list of active reviewers will be made public in [https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/community/reviewers](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/community/reviewers) and will include recommendations on their areas of expertise/knowledge. Reviewers should self-assign PRs they are actively reviewing and publicly coordinate with other reviewers in \#pr-reviews. 

## Appointment and Development

Candidates should demonstrate a sustained record of useful reviews, sound engineering judgment, constructive communication, and familiarity with vLLM’s contribution standards. Deep ownership of a subsystem is not required. A reviewer should be nominated by 2 committers from different organizations. Committers should post in \#committers when nominating reviewers.

Before being nominated a general rule of thumb (not a hard requirement) are the reviewer should have either 15 merged PRs and have reviewed\* 30 PRs OR have reviewed\* 45 PRs.

\* “Reviewed” implies the reviewer gave a substantive review and the PR went on to some kind of resolution (merged or closed)

New reviewers should receive feedback and mentorship from committers. A private Slack channel will be set up to facilitate communication between Reviewers and Committers, including review questions, feedback, and coordination on PRs.

First serving as a reviewer will become the standard path for new committer appointments. This establishes demonstrated review service as part of the path to merge authority. While this is not a hard requirement and there may be exceptions we do consider this the standard and preferred path.

## Rollout and Evaluation

Start with a small cohort of trusted reviewers working across the project (initially \~50, potentially scaling up to 2x active committers).

Things to assess:

- Time to first substantive review and time waiting for final committer review.  
- Review quality, i.e. committer effort required to bring reviewed contributions to a final decision.  
- CI queue pressure.  
- Backlog size and age, distinguishing merged PRs from closed or withdrawn PRs.

Success is a sustained increase in effective review capacity: contributions receive useful feedback sooner, review responsibility is distributed across more trusted contributors, and the backlog declines without compromising quality or overloading reviewers and CI.

Community members should have access to a directory of which reviewers to reach out to for different topics, to enable them collaborate effectively on slack channels such as \#pr-reviews

## Precedents

Several established projects distribute review responsibilities beyond contributors with final acceptance or merge authority:

- [**Kubernetes**](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/main/community-membership.md#reviewer) distinguishes Reviewers, who assess contribution quality and correctness, from Approvers, who authorize acceptance.  
- [**containerd**](https://github.com/containerd/.project/blob/main/GOVERNANCE.md#reviewers) has explicit Reviewer and Committer tiers. Reviewers’ LGTMs count toward merge requirements, but reviewers do not have write access. Reviewer service is part of the path toward committership.  
- [**Python / CPython**](https://devguide.python.org/triage/triage-team/) has a formal Triage Team whose responsibilities include reviewing PRs, assisting contributors, and involving core developers. Its stated purpose is to provide timely feedback and reduce core-developer workload.

### Proposed Change.

## Implementation

The implementation must give reviewer decisions meaningful visibility while keeping final acceptance and merging with committers.

### Option A \[Selected\]: Native GitHub reviews with restricted merging

Give Reviewers Write access, and restrict updates to protected branches to the Committer team and authorized bots. This gives reviewer feedback native GitHub review authority, including blocking requests for changes under the configured review rules.

This option uses GitHub’s existing review interface without requiring a bot to recognize reviewer approvals. It does grant broader write privileges, including on unprotected branches. All relevant branches and merge paths must therefore be covered by the restrictions, and the configuration must be verified before rollout. GitHub documents these capabilities in its [repository role permissions](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/managing-user-access-to-your-organizations-repositories/managing-repository-roles/repository-roles-for-an-organization) and [branch protection rules](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/about-protected-branches).


<details>

<summary>Other options considered</summary>
### Option B: Triage access with a bot-managed review check

Give Reviewers Triage access and use a bot to recognize reviews from the designated Reviewer team. The bot would publish a named status check, such as “Reviewer approval,” and track unresolved requests for changes.

The bot would make Reviewer approvals visible as a readiness signal without requiring them for merge. It would separately track unresolved Reviewer requests for changes so those concerns must be resolved or explicitly adjudicated by a Committer. A bot-generated check would not change the permissions or appearance of the native GitHub review. This option preserves the absence of repository write access but requires automation that handles team membership, updated commits, dismissed reviews, outstanding objections, and explicit committer resolutions correctly.

#### Review Automation Options

##### Prow

[Kubernetes’ Prow](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/prow) provides an established command model:

- `/cc @username`: request review from a contributor.  
- `/assign @username`: assign responsibility for a PR.  
- `/lgtm`: record that a change looks good following review.  
- `/lgtm cancel`: withdraw that review signal.  
- `/approve`: record final acceptance by an authorized approver.  
- `/hold`: prevent automatic merging while an outstanding concern is resolved.

For vLLM, `/lgtm` could represent a trusted Reviewer or Committer’s completed review, while `/approve` would remain restricted to Committers. Committers could perform both steps directly. Prow can also translate native GitHub approval and request-changes reviews into LGTM label changes.

Prow’s default authorization does not exactly match this proposal: `/lgtm` is generally available to repository collaborators, while `/approve` uses OWNERS files.

##### Mergeable

[Mergeable](https://mergeable.readthedocs.io/en/latest/validators/approval.html) can react to native GitHub reviews through `pull_request_review.*`, count approvals from designated teams, and publish a review check. Its [approval validator](https://github.com/mergeability/mergeable/blob/master/lib/validators/approvals.js) filters reviews by team membership or username without requiring write access, making it a candidate for recognizing Triage-only Reviewer approvals. Reviewers could use GitHub’s normal Approve and Request changes actions, with a passing check signaling readiness for committer review. 

##### A lightweight GitHub App or GitHub Actions workflow

Custom automation could recognize native reviews or a small command set from explicit Reviewer and Committer teams, publish review status, and integrate with existing CI labels and triggers. This offers the most direct fit for Option B but makes vLLM responsible for maintaining the implementation.

</details>

### CI access

The implementation should verify the behavior of labels and CI triggers and build on existing controls where possible. CI access should allow reviewers to unblock ready contributions without routinely involving a committer. Reviewers should assess readiness before triggering expensive jobs and avoid unnecessary reruns. Faster review may increase CI demand even if incoming PR volume stays constant. The rollout should monitor queue times and resource use.

title: [RFC]: DeepSeek-V4 Performance Optimization on ROCm (Phase Two)
body:
## Motivation.

> Continue working on phase one: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/41820.

DeepSeek-V4 introduces CSA (Compressed Sparse Attention, `compress_ratio=4`), HCA layers, and a large MoE backbone. A side-by-side trace comparison of the vLLM decode path against vLLM-ATOM on ROCm shows that vLLM still leaves measurable performance on the table. The gaps cluster into three areas:

1. **Unfused mHC kernels.** vLLM runs `mhc_post` and `mhc_pre` as separate kernels, and `mhc_pre_big_fuse` + `add_rmsnorm_quant` as two kernels, while ATOM fuses each pair into a single kernel (`mhc_fused_post_pre` and `mhc_pre_big_fuse_rmsnorm`). Every extra kernel launch on the decode critical path costs launch latency and cache/register thrash.
2. **Serial execution where overlap is possible.** ATOM forks auxiliary HIP streams to run compressor GEMMs (CSA pre-attention), SWA KV insertion (HCA), and the MoE router/shared experts concurrently with the main stream. vLLM executes all of these serially.
3. **Slower attention support kernels.** ATOM replaces the vLLM CSA top-k selection kernels and the post-attention batched GEMMs (`torch.mm` + `manual_unroll`) with dedicated optimized kernels (e.g., `batched_gemm_bf16_kernel`).

An earlier attempt at closing gap #2 — PR #51794, which enables three-stream overlap for CSA pre-attention — is currently a draft: the overlapped region itself is faster when there is no bubble, but some ranks see a much slower tail all-reduce due to inter-rank latency jitter. The un-optimized kernels running in the parallel streams contend for hardware resources and desynchronize ranks. This suggests the correct order of work is: **replace the kernels with ATOM's optimized versions first, then enable stream overlap on top of them.**

## Proposed Change.

Port the ATOM-optimized decode path into vLLM's ROCm DeepSeek-V4 implementation, using the ATOM trace as the reference for each change. The work is organized per module:

### CSA:

- [x] **Fuse mHC kernels:** merge `mhc_post` + `mhc_pre` into `mhc_fused_post_pre`, and `mhc_pre_big_fuse` + `add_rmsnorm_quant` into `mhc_pre_big_fuse_rmsnorm`. #52737 @shen-shanshan 
- [x] **Fuse SWA q/kv RMSNorm and q FP8 group quant:** #53540 @shen-shanshan 
- [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53838
- [x] **Pre-attention three-stream overlap:** Before the input GEMMs, fork three HIP streams: (1) **default stream**: fused wqa+wkv GEMM → q/kv RMSNorm → wq_b → qnorm/RoPE → SWA KV insert; (2) **aux stream 0**: main-compressor wkv_gate GEMM → compress kernels (compressed KV cache write); (3) **aux stream 1**: indexer-compressor wkv_gate GEMM → K-cache write. After the join, the indexer weights GEMM, the indexer q-side (wq_b + fused q RoPE+quant), the sparse indexer op (top-k selection), and the MLA attention run serially on the main stream. Each aux stream is a self-contained chain starting from `hidden_states`, so no fine-grained cross-stream dependencies are required. **This item stays disabled (draft) until the kernels in the parallel streams are replaced with ATOM's**.

title: [Bug]: An Anthropic messages test is not compatible with Anthropic SDK 1.x
body:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py vllm 0.28.0, 0.29.0 ```text Your output of `python collect_env.py` here ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug `tests/entrypoints/anthropic/test_messages.py::test_anthropic_streaming_cache_usage` passes `temperature=0.0` as a keyword argument to `AsyncMessages.create()`. That works on Anthropic Python SDK 0.x, but breaks on 1.x: ```text TypeError: AsyncMessages.create() got an unexpected keyword argument 'temperature' ``` This is a client-side SDK change, not a vLLM serving bug. Anthropic SDK 1.0 removed temperature / top_p / top_k from messages.create(), messages.stream(), and messages.parse(). Official migration notes: https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python/blob/main/MIGRATION.md#removed-deprecated-request-parameters Those sampling fields are gone from the method signature, not from the HTTP API. For older models that still honor them (including this test's served name claude-3-7-sonnet-latest), the documented replacement is extra_body: ```python # before client.messages.create(..., temperature=0.2) # after client.messages.create(..., extra_body={"temperature": 0.2}) ``` extra_body is merged into the JSON body by the SDK. vLLM already declares temperature on AnthropicMessagesRequest, so the server keeps parsing it as a normal field. No serving-side extra_body handling is required. vLLM depends on anthropic >= 0.71.0 (requirements/common.txt) with no <1 cap, so CI / downstream installs can resolve either 0.x or 1.x. extra_body exists on both generations, so this keeps the test working for both, but temperature= would get TypeError on 1.x. This test only asserts streaming prefix-cache usage (cache_read / cache_creation on message_delta). It does not inspect generated text, so it is indifferent to greedy vs default sampling. Dropping temperature entirely would also fix the TypeError This PR https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57780 keeps greedy via extra_body to stay closest to the original request. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC] LoRA Adapter Lifecycle for RL Training
body:
# [RFC] LoRA Adapter Lifecycle for RL Training

## Problem

RL + LoRA workflows have three vLLM-side issues:

1. **sleep/wake crash**: Level-2 sleep with `enable_lora=True` crashes with KeyError — LoRA adapter parameters are not in cumem's tag set ([#39934](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/39934))
2. **Adapter-only sync missing**: frameworks must merge LoRA → send full weights → unmerge. Adapter-only sync (send only LoRA delta, load via vLLM's LoRA serving) would eliminate the merge round-trip ([trl#5975](https://github.com/huggingface/trl/issues/5975))
3. **LoRA + MoE mismatch**: logprob divergence between training and inference grows with LoRA rank on MoE models (Qwen3.6, GLM-4.7-Flash) ([SkyRL#1776](https://github.com/NovaSky-AI/SkyRL/issues/1776))

## Downstream demand

- [trl#5975](https://github.com/huggingface/trl/issues/5975): Adapter-only vLLM LoRA sync for GRPO/AsyncGRPO
- [SkyRL#1776](https://github.com/NovaSky-AI/SkyRL/issues/1776): LoRA + MoE inference mismatch investigation
- [verl#6782](https://github.com/verl-project/verl/issues/6782): Qwen3.5-27B LoRA GRPO — vLLM never emits EOS with rank=64

## Exit criterion

- sleep/wake + LoRA (#39934) no longer crashes
- Adapter-only sync path available (no full-weight merge required)

## Feedback Period

Two weeks from posting.

title: [Bug]: Whisper `verbose_json` silently drops the words after the last complete segment at every chunk cut (long audio); `json`/`text` keep them
body:
### Your current environment

vLLM 0.25.1 (`vllm/vllm-openai:v0.25.1`), `openai/whisper-large-v3`, RTX 5070 Ti, `--dtype float32` (also reproduces in float16), `/v1/audio/transcriptions`.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

For audio longer than `max_audio_clip_s` (30 s) vLLM splits it into contiguous chunks at the quietest point of the last second of each window (`split_audio`). When that cut lands mid-sentence, Whisper decoded **with timestamp tokens** (which `verbose_json` requires) closes its last complete segment and emits nothing for the audio after it. The words between that last segment end and the cut are lost from `segments` **and** from the `text` field of the verbose response, which is assembled from segments. `response_format=json` / `text` decode with `<|notimestamps|>` and keep those words.

This is not the timestamp drift of #32588 and not the split-point scan bug of #52927 (PR #52927 changes *where* the cut lands; the loss happens whenever a cut lands inside speech at all).

**Minimal reproduction** (synthetic speech, no data-privacy concerns; the split is deterministic):

```bash
espeak-ng -v en-us -s 160 -w long.wav "Chief complaint. The patient is a sixty two year old woman who presents for follow up of type two diabetes and hypertension. She reports good adherence to metformin one thousand milligrams twice daily and losartan fifty milligrams daily. History of present illness. Over the past three months she has noted increased fatigue and occasional blurry vision in the mornings. She denies polyuria, polydipsia, chest pain, or shortness of breath. Home glucose readings range from one hundred thirty to one hundred ninety milligrams per deciliter. Review of systems. Positive for fatigue and intermittent headaches."
ffmpeg -y -i long.wav -ac 1 -ar 16000 -sample_fmt s16 -t 30 first30.wav      # exactly one 30 s window
for fmt in json verbose_json; do
  curl -s -F "file=@first30.wav;type=audio/wav" -F model=openai/whisper-large-v3 -F response_format=$fmt \
       http://localhost:8000/v1/audio/transcriptions | python3 -c "import json,sys; t=json.load(sys.stdin)['text']; print('$fmt', len(t.split()), 'words:', t[-120:])"
done
```

Observed:

```
json          67 words: ... chest pain, or shortness of breath. Home glucose readings range  Fru-
verbose_json  59 words: ... occasional blurry vision in the mornings. She denies polyuria, polydipsia, chest pain,  FRU-
```

`verbose_json`'s last real segment ends at 26.4 s; the 3.6 s of speech before the 30 s cut ("or shortness of breath. Home glucose readings range") is gone. On a 977 s pause-free clip this happened at 4 of 32 chunk boundaries (11.3 s of audio, ~1.4 % of the words); on a real 16-minute dictation with natural pauses, 2 of the cuts still landed inside speech.

### Why

The reference implementations (openai/whisper, faster-whisper) decode a 30 s window, take the timestamp of the last complete segment, and **seek the next window to that timestamp**, re-decoding the tail with fresh context. vLLM pre-cuts the audio into fixed contiguous chunks before decoding, so the tail after the last segment is never decoded by anyone. Feeding previous-chunk context (#25750, PR #20249) would improve accuracy but does not recover those words either.

### Proposed fixes (either would do)

1. **Seek-based chunking for timestamp requests**: decode chunk *i*; if its output ends with a closed segment at *t* < chunk end, start chunk *i+1* at *t* (not at the energy-based cut). This is what the reference decoders do and makes the loss structurally impossible. It serializes chunks, which is fine for verbose requests (they already are sequential in the offline path).
2. **Cheaper mitigation**: when the model's output for a chunk ends without a closing timestamp *or* ends more than N s before the chunk end, re-decode the uncovered tail `[t, chunk_end)` as an extra request and append it as a segment.

Workaround we use today: cut the audio at silences into ≤ 28 s pieces client-side and send each piece separately (the server never chunks), then offset the segment times. Works, but every verbose_json user of long audio is hitting this without knowing.

title: [Feature] [KV Offload] Support sharing SimpleCPUOffload prefix caches across local DP replicas
body:
# Motivation

`SimpleCPUOffloadConnector` (#37160) keeps a private CPU prefix cache per
DP replica. Unlike the native `OffloadingConnector`, the Simple connector is
agnostic to KV organization and adapts to day-0 models without per-model
integration, which makes it a natural fit for throughput-oriented DP-heavy
deployments (e.g. 8×H100 with DP8/TP1/EP). In such deployments each
replica's CPU KV pool is small, and identical prefixes are recomputed
whenever a request is routed to a different local replica, even though a
completed CPU copy exists on the same host. Sharing the local CPU pool would
let these deployments draw on a larger combined KV pool instead of many
small private ones.

Measured on a diagnostic DP4/TP1/EP topology (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, two hosts,
two logical workers sharing each physical GB10 GPU — timings are diagnostic,
not production throughput numbers). Routing a repeated ~6K-token prefix to a
peer replica costs **14.41 s TTFT (full recompute)**; with shared offload it
costs **5.22 s (91.7% of prompt tokens restored via external KV transfer)** —
a 63.8% reduction.

# Proposed approach

Opt-in `cpu_offload_shared=true` in `kv_connector_extra_config`:
- Reuse `SharedOffloadRegion` (#50094), `BlockPool` hash/LRU, `ChunkStatus`, connector handshake; no new copy backend or allocator
- Fixed per-writer slot partitions; shared publication index + `flock` on the metadata region fd; reader references protect slots during peer DMA
- Node-local only; eager offloading; any TP×DP combination (each TP coordinate shares its own KV shard pool); startup fails closed on incompatible hash/model/layout
- PP/DCP/PCP beyond 1 is not supported yet; extending to those is desirable follow-up work, not required for the initial version

# Context

- Duplicate check against open PRs: #53474, #53073, #47324, #57418, #43483,
  #57422, #54743, #52921 — none publishes prefix hashes across DP schedulers.
- No code dependency on #53474 or #53073: peer discovery uses the existing
  `in_the_same_node_as` and region APIs. #53474 is actively reshaping the native connector's region geometry, so this feature deliberately avoids
  coupling to it; overlapping files (worker.py, docs) should need only routine rebases.

title: [Bug]: cutlass_scaled_mm_supports_block_fp8 excludes SM89 (Ada Lovelace) despite native FP8 tensor core support
body:
### Your current environment

**Environment:**
- GPU: NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada Generation (SM 8.9)
- vLLM: 0.29.0
- CUDA: 13.4
- Model: Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 (block-quantized FP8, 128×128 blocks)

### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Description:**
cutlass_block_fp8_supported() returns False on Ada Lovelace (SM89), causing block-quantized FP8 checkpoints to fall through the kernel priority list in _POSSIBLE_FP8_BLOCK_KERNELS all the way to MarlinFP8ScaledMMLinearKernel — bypassing CUTLASS entirely, even though:

Non-block FP8 CUTLASS is supported on this card: cutlass_fp8_supported() == True
Ada Lovelace has native FP8 tensor core hardware, and vLLM's own docs state FP8 W8A8 is officially supported on "Hopper and Ada Lovelace" (https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/features/quantization/fp8/)

Bisecting ops.cutlass_scaled_mm_supports_block_fp8() directly shows a hard floor at SM90:
- 80 -> False
- 86 -> False
- 89 -> False
- 90 -> True
- 100 -> True

**Question:** Is this a genuine CUTLASS-library-level limitation (e.g. block-scaled grouped GEMM requiring Hopper-specific TMA multicast at the collective-builder level, similar to the SM_120/SM_121 CUTLASS MoE gap in #43507), or is SM89 support for block-scaled CUTLASS GEMM simply not yet wired up in vLLM's compiled extension?

If it's the latter, this is a meaningful gap for anyone running block-quantized FP8 checkpoints (increasingly common — DeepSeek-style 128×128 block scales) on Ada workstation cards (RTX 6000 Ada, L40S, RTX 4090), since it silently falls back to Marlin's weight-only dequant path rather than using the card's native FP8 compute.

**Repro:**
```
from vllm import _custom_ops as ops
for cap in [80, 86, 89, 90, 100]:
    print(cap, ops.cutlass_scaled_mm_supports_block_fp8(cap))
```
