title: [Feature]: Improve engine RPC failure handling and shutdown
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

When one worker returns an RPC error, other workers may still have replies pending. Returning immediately can leave those replies for the next call, while waiting without a deadline can block indefinitely. If reply collection cannot finish, the executor must stop accepting work, callers must receive the failure, and workers must be cleaned up.

This proposal connects reply collection, failure propagation, and cleanup around two outcomes:

```text
worker error response
  -> collect the remaining expected replies within a shared reply collection deadline
     |-- complete: return the error; preserve reply correspondence
     |             -> caller may continue where the operation permits recovery
     +-- timeout: fail the executor and notify EngineCore
                   |-- fail pending calls and reject new RPCs
                   +-- run Core and worker cleanup
                       -> finish cleanup or let the process manager enforce its shutdown deadline
```

The timeout branch is deliberately conservative: a reply missing at the reply collection deadline makes the executor unusable, even if the worker is only delayed. This extends terminal-failure handling to RPC response timeouts, using the existing executor-failure callback and Core/process-manager shutdown path. Both outcomes depend on the following four changes.

### 1. Finish the failed call's reply collection

Worker RPC replies are matched to calls by queue order. If RPC A returns after reading one worker's error, RPC B can consume an unread reply from A:

```text
Worker 0 reply queue: [RPC B reply]
Worker 1 reply queue: [RPC A reply] [RPC B reply]
                          ^
                  incorrectly consumed by RPC B
```

Record the first error encountered in reply-queue order, then finish consuming **one reply from each worker selected for RPC A**, counting both successful and failed replies. Return the recorded error after collection completes, leaving replies for later RPCs untouched. RPC A still fails, but a subsequent operation can read its own replies.

### 2. Bound waiting for stragglers

Collecting those remaining replies requires a limit on waiting. Another worker may be a straggler, still alive but slow to reply, or may never respond.

After the first worker error, apply one reply collection deadline. Share the remaining time across all selected workers and receive stages, preserving any earlier caller deadline.

If the reply collection deadline expires, fail the executor and block both queued and new RPCs from reusing the response queues.

### 3. Propagate terminal failure to waiting callers

Blocking further RPCs does not release callers already waiting for results. Fail queued worker RPC futures when the executor becomes unusable. Client utility calls need separate handling because they wait on their own futures.

The client already detects engine death through engine-dead notifications and, for managed local processes, process monitoring. Receiver errors are forwarded to the generation output queue, which utility callers are not waiting on. Setting the engine-dead flag or stopping the receiver leaves their futures pending.

When the output receiver stops, fail all pending sync/async utility futures so those callers receive the failure too. Cover cancellation before the async receiver starts, and leave already-cancelled calls cancelled.

### 4. Let worker cleanup finish after failure is reported

Failure notification can also trigger shutdown while cleanup is still in progress. EngineCore reports fatal failure before its own teardown completes, and a client or process manager may react by sending SIGTERM. If Core has already restored the default signal handling, that signal can terminate it before worker cleanup finishes.

Ignore additional SIGTERM and SIGINT during Core cleanup. The process manager retains its existing shutdown deadline and can force termination of the process tree if cleanup does not finish in time.

These changes affect shared executor, client, and shutdown paths. Automatic retries, RPC identifiers, and new cross-node or parent-death detection protocols are outside this proposal.

### Alternatives

Treat every worker RPC error as terminal and restart the engine, without collecting the remaining replies for reuse. This simplifies reply handling but gives up recovery when all replies could be collected and a follow-up operation would be safe.

### Additional context

### Example Scenario
Consider an RL controller attempting `wake_up()` after a failed level-1 sleep in the same engine:

```text
Worker 0: releases some allocations, then returns an error
Worker 1: completes sleep
```

Inference must remain paused until the required allocations are restored and all required wake operations succeed. Otherwise, a successful-looking wake can allow the next forward pass to access released memory.

This also requires preserving `sleeping_tags` when the sleep RPC raises. Without that state, `wake_up()` can take the already-awake path and skip restoration. The shared RPC handling then ensures that the wake result comes from that wake's own replies. Together, these changes produce the following behavior:

```text
partial sleep failure; inference stays paused
  -> collect this sleep's expected replies within the reply collection deadline
     |-- complete: return the sleep error with restoration state preserved
     |             -> controller chooses wake_up()
     |             -> workers perform their required restoration
     |             -> collect this wake's own replies
     |             -> resume inference only if all required wake operations succeed
     +-- timeout: fail executor and pending calls; proceed through managed shutdown
                   -> controller receives an error and can restart or stop
                   -> no inference resumes on the failed executor
```

The controller still decides whether to request recovery. These changes do not make every allocator failure recoverable.

### Future plan

These guarantees provide a basis for automatic recovery policies. The following directions are outside this proposal:

- **Per-worker outcomes.** Report structured outcomes for each selected worker, including its rank, failure details, and whether a reply was received. This would give recovery policies more information than the first exception returned to the caller.
- **Bounded automatic recovery for partial failures.** For operations with defined retry and restoration semantics, attempt recovery on affected workers where the backend permits it. Keep inference paused until all required workers are ready and their shared state is consistent. Restart the engine if recovery is unsafe or exceeds its budget.
- **Recovery after worker loss.** Explore selective worker replacement. This requires backend support to rebuild the affected communication group and restore consistent model and cache state. An executor failed by a response timeout remains terminal; recovery must establish a fresh executor or use a separately designed channel reinitialization protocol before accepting new work.

### Roadmap alignment

This proposal contributes to the **production stability and failure ergonomics** goal under SIG Core in [#48168: vLLM Roadmap Q3 2026](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48168).

The sleep/wake scenario also supports **Section 1.2 Scheduler (Sleep/Wake/Drain)** in [#48314: 2026 Q3 vLLM and RL](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48314), tracked in [#48311: Engine Sleep/Wake/Drain Lifecycle for RL](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48311).

### Related work

| Proposal section | Existing work |
| --- | --- |
| **1. Finish reply collection** | [#49972](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/49972), [PR #49976](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49976) |
| **3. Fail waiting callers** | [PR #56416](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56416) |

title: [Feature]: Fast Start For vLLM
body:
## Overview

Fast Start reduces vLLM startup time by avoiding repeated checkpoint loading, weight processing, and kernel autotuning during engine restarts and scaling events.

The core design uses a persistent per-GPU weight daemon. The daemon loads and processes model weights once, keeps sharded weights in GPU memory, and exposes them to new vLLM engines through CUDA IPC or a multi-node transport.

When a compatible cache is unavailable, vLLM falls back to the existing checkpoint loader.

## Design Goals

- Reuse processed GPU weights across engine instances.
- Support TP, PP, EP, multi-node deployments, and MTP.
- Support quantized formats including FP8 and FP4.
- Cache autotune results with hardware- and version-aware keys.
- Preserve correctness through strict cache validation.
- Provide a reliable fallback path for cache misses and failures.

## Cache Validation

Cache entries are identified using model and checkpoint identity, quantization configuration, parallelism settings, GPU architecture, vLLM protocol version, and other relevant runtime metadata.

Incompatible entries must never be silently reused. Cache misses, stale daemon connections, and validation failures produce diagnostics and fall back to the normal loading path when enabled.

## Roadmap

### Weight Daemon (core)
- [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54921
- [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56047

### Parallelism
- [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57386
- [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55477
- [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55490
- [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55468

### Quantization
- [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55465
- [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57316

### Model & Memory
- [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57312
- [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57320
- [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57298

## CLI support
- [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56680
- [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57577


## Success Criteria

- Warm engine startup avoids repeated checkpoint loading.
- Cached and regular loading produce equivalent model outputs.
- Cache failures do not compromise correctness or availability.
- Startup, cache-hit, fallback, transfer, and autotune timings are observable.

title: [Bug]: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: SimpleCPUOffloadConnector crashes with `assert block_size % hash_block_size == 0` (block_size=8, hash_block_size=32)
body:
### Your current environment

## Environment

- Hardware: 8 × H100 80GB (HBM3), CUDA 13
- vLLM version: `0.1.dev20904+g179dd0fa9` (image `vllm/vllm-openai:deepseekv41-flash-0909`)
- Model: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (fp8, hybrid KV cache: MLA full-attention group @ block_size 32 + SWA/circular-buffer group @ block_size 8; DSpark MTP speculative decoding)
- Python 3.12, TP=8, EP=8

### 🐛 Describe the bug

## Summary

Serving `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` (hybrid KV: full-attention MLA + sliding-window/circular-buffer groups) with the `SimpleCPUOffloadConnector` crashes the EngineCore on the **first scheduled request** with:

```
(EngineCore pid=536) [ASSERT-DEBUG] resolve_block_hashes: block_size=8, hash_block_size=32, modulo=8   <-- our instrumented print, see note below
(EngineCore pid=536) ERROR ... assert block_size % hash_block_size == 0
AssertionError
```

(The `[ASSERT-DEBUG]` line is **not** stock vLLM output — we volume-mounted a patched `kv_cache_utils.py` into the container that prints `block_size`/`hash_block_size`/modulo just before the assert, since the bare `AssertionError` carries no values. Stock vLLM produces only the assert line; details in *Extra context*.)

Note `block_size (8) < hash_block_size (32)` — the call asks `resolve_block_hashes` to view 32-token-granularity hashes at a *finer* 8-token granularity, but the function only supports the coarsening direction (`block_size >= hash_block_size`, enforced by the divisibility assert). With 8 < 32 the assert `8 % 32 == 0` can never hold, so the crash is deterministic on the first request.

## Deploy command (paths/ports/keys elided)

```bash
docker run --gpus all --privileged --ipc=host --net=host \
  <model-volume-mounts> \
  vllm/vllm-openai:deepseekv41-flash-0909 \
  vllm serve <model-path> \
  --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v41 \
  --enable-expert-parallel \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
  --max-num-seqs 32 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 \
  --tool-call-parser deepseek_v41 \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --reasoning-parser deepseek_v41 \
  --mm-encoder-tp-mode data \
  --compilation-config '{"cudagraph_capture_sizes": [1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56, 64, 72, 80, 88, 96, 104, 112, 120, 128, 136, 144, 152, 160]}' \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":5,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic","rejection_sample_method":"block","enable_adaptive_verification":true}' \
  --enable-prompt-tokens-details \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"SimpleCPUOffloadConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_extra_config":{"cpu_bytes_to_use_per_rank":118111600640,"lazy_offload":false}}'
```

Note on `--compilation-config`: the default cudagraph capture sizes (up to 512 with profiling) OOM on this model+hardware, so capture sizes are explicitly capped at 160.

## Reproduction

1. Start the server with the command above. Startup completes normally (weights load, CPU offload pool allocates, CUDA graphs capture, "Application startup complete").
2. Send any request that triggers KV offload bookkeeping (e.g. a chat completion with a long prompt).
3. EngineCore crashes immediately in the scheduler step:

```
(EngineCore pid=536) [ASSERT-DEBUG] resolve_block_hashes: block_size=8, hash_block_size=32, modulo=8
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../vllm/v1/engine/core.py", line 1430, in run_busy_loop
    self._process_engine_step()
  File ".../vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py", line 1373, in schedule
    meta = self._build_kv_connector_meta(self.connector, scheduler_output)
  File ".../vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/simple_cpu_offload_connector.py", line 268, in build_connector_meta
    return self.scheduler_manager.build_connector_meta(scheduler_output)
  File ".../vllm/v1/simple_kv_offload/manager.py", line 453, in build_connector_meta
    store_gpu, store_cpu, store_req_ids, store_meta = self.prepare_store_specs(...)
  File ".../vllm/v1/simple_kv_offload/manager.py", line 523, in prepare_store_specs
    return self._prepare_eager_store_specs(scheduler_output)
  File ".../vllm/v1/simple_kv_offload/manager.py", line 638, in _prepare_eager_store_specs
    self._select_eager_blocks_to_store(state, block_ids_by_group)
  File ".../vllm/v1/simple_kv_offload/manager.py", line 720, in _select_eager_blocks_to_store
    resolved_hashes = resolve_block_hashes(
  File ".../vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py", line 2788, in resolve_block_hashes
    assert block_size % hash_block_size == 0
AssertionError
```

## Root cause analysis

The offload path mixes up per-group block geometry with the global hash granularity:

1. `resolve_kv_cache_block_sizes()` (`vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py:~726-792`) computes for multi-group models:
   - `hash_block_size = gcd(group_block_sizes)` over **prefix-cacheable** groups — for DSV4.1-Flash: gcd(32, 8) = 8? No — in our crash the resolved `hash_block_size=32` and the group's `group_size=8`, meaning the SWA/circular-buffer group (block_size 8) was **excluded** from the hashing_sizes GCD (its `prefix_cacheable` is False for `CircularBufferSpec`/Kpool-tail style specs), so `hash_block_size` followed the full-attention group (32).
   - `SimpleCPUOffloadScheduler` stores this as `self.hash_block_size` and asserts `self.block_size % self.hash_block_size == 0` at init (manager.py:129) — which passes because `self.block_size` is the **scheduler** block size (LCM), not any single group's size.

2. At request time, `_select_eager_blocks_to_store()` (manager.py:720) iterates **all** KV cache groups — including the non-prefix-cacheable SWA group — and calls:
   ```python
   resolved_hashes = resolve_block_hashes(
       request.block_hashes, self.hash_block_size, group_size)
   ```
   with `group_size = 8` (the SWA group) and `hash_block_size = 32`.

3. `resolve_block_hashes()` (kv_cache_utils.py:2770-2789) only supports viewing fine hashes at a **coarser** granularity (`block_size >= hash_block_size`, enforced by the assert). Receiving `block_size(8) < hash_block_size(32)` violates its contract.

Two contributing bugs:
- `_select_eager_blocks_to_store` passes a group-local block size into a function whose contract assumes the caller wants a **scheduler-level** view; for groups with `block_size < hash_block_size` the call is meaningless (there are no per-group hashes at 8-token granularity — hashes only exist at 32-token boundaries).
- The init-time assert (manager.py:129) checks the wrong invariant (`scheduler_block_size % hash_block_size == 0`), which is trivially true and hides the per-group mismatch until the first request.

## Suggested fixes

Any of these would unblock DSV4.1-Flash-class hybrid models; (1)+(2) together are probably the right combination:

1. **Skip hash resolution for non-prefix-cacheable groups** in `_select_eager_blocks_to_store` (and the lazy variant): the SWA/circular-buffer group's KV is windowed/evicted anyway, so offloading it by content hash is not meaningful. Only resolve hashes for groups whose `kv_cache_spec.prefix_cacheable` is True and whose `block_size >= hash_block_size`.

2. **Clamp per-group block size in the manager**: when calling `resolve_block_hashes`, pass `max(group_size, self.hash_block_size)` or round `group_size` up to a multiple of `hash_block_size`, mirroring what `BlockHashListWithBlockSize` does for the coarser direction.

3. **Harden `resolve_block_hashes`**: replace the bare assert with a descriptive error, and/or support the `block_size < hash_block_size` direction by returning the finest available view with an offset warning — though semantically this case should be prevented by the caller (fix 1).

## Extra context

- Same model + same image **without** `--kv-transfer-config` serves and benchmarks fine (stable under 100K-prefix prefix-repetition load, and single-batch decode TPS ~330-350 tok/s with DSpark), so the regression is specific to the CPU offload connector path.
- An equivalent sglang deployment with hierarchical cache (`--enable-hierarchical-cache`, host pool ~127 GB/rank paged) serves the same workload without issue, for comparison.
- We patched `kv_cache_utils.py` inside the container with a debug print before the assert to capture the failing values (`block_size=8, hash_block_size=32, modulo=8`), which is how the numbers above were obtained.

---
*This issue report was generated with AI assistance.*

title: [torch.compile] Proper PassManager infrastructure
body:
### Motivation

Currently, we bundle custom torch.compile passes using the `PostGradPassManager`. This manager is set as the `current_platform.pass_key` (default: `"post_grad_custom_post_pass"`), and individual passes within it are enabled/disabled using individual flags. This lacks scalability and control: every additional pass requires a new flag, which we often skip for utility passes (leaving no way to disable them). Platforms also have to choose a single `pass_key` as opposed to plugging into multiple points in the PyTorch compilation pipeline.

This inhibits debugging from the CLI, requiring manual code modifications. It also requires platforms to reimplement a lot of the pass management (enablement, cache hash, etc.). Another example is vLLM-Spyre, which currently plugs into `"post_grad_custom_post_pass"` for custom codegen transformations, colliding with the default vLLM pass manager.

### Proposal

We should create a base `PassManager` class, which can handle invoking multiple passes and properly exposes a `uuid()` method to Inductor/AOTAutograd caching. We should also add a way to manually specify the full list of passes on the command line/in Python. Current flags can stick around and be used to produce this list by default. Passes should also be refactored to use 0-arg constructors by default (and read `VllmConfig` using `get_current_vllm_config()`) - that way OOT passes can integrate into this list more easily. This will also allow IR passes to move into the `vllm/ir` folder and remove their dependence on vLLM.

### Timeline
This is not urgent and should probably wait until torch 2.12 when `pre_grad_custom_pass` becomes a proper `CustomGraphPass`. Depending on interest from OOT backends, this can be prioritized earlier.

title: [RFC]: Replace Hardcoded Device Strings with current_platform and Implement Linting
body:
### Motivation.

Currently, the vLLM codebase contains numerous instances of hardcoded device strings such as "cuda", "cuda:0", and .to("cuda"). This hinders our goal of being a truly multi-platform LLM engine (supporting ROCm, TPU, Gaudi/HPU, etc.) 

Hardcoding "cuda" creates several issues:
Portability: Developers porting vLLM to new hardware must manually find and replace strings, which is error-prone.
Consistency: Some parts of the code use cuda, while others use current_platform. We need a single source of truth.
Future-Proofing: As we move toward better abstraction, the device type should be a property of the environment, not a static string in the logic.

for those that want to limit the test on cuda or specific platform, we better use decorators to skip it on other platform instead of giving a hardcode device string. Refer https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/39158

### Proposed Change.

1. Use @pytest.mark.device_type(DEVICE_TYPE) and conftest.py hook for single gpu and single process cases
```python
 # 1. current usgae:
def test_case():
    tensor_a = torch.tensor([1, 2, 3], device='cuda')
    
# 2. unify hardcode device type  
DEVICE_TYPE = current_platform.device_type
def test_case():
    tensor_a = torch.tensor([1, 2, 3], device='DEVICE_TYPE')
    
# 3. refactor by with torch.device, while this may have indent issue, less readable for me
DEVICE_TYPE = current_platform.device_type
def test_case():
    with torch.device(DEVICE_TYPE):
        tensor_a = torch.tensor([1, 2, 3])
        
# 4. define a specific pytest marker for torch.device context manager 
DEVICE_TYPE = current_platform.device_type
@pytest.mark.device_type(DEVICE_TYPE) # will be same to 3
def test_case():
    tensor_a = torch.tensor([1, 2, 3])
```    

2. Directly replace the hardcode string with DEVICE_TYPE(inferred from current_platform.device_type) for multiprocess and multigpu cases, most under tests/distributed and tests/compile/distributed
- use DEVICE_TYPE (inferred from current_platform.device_type) replace hardcode cuda device
- use DEVICES ([f"{DEVICE_TYPE}:{i}" for i in range(1 if current_platform.device_count() == 1 else 2)]) replace CUDA_DEVICES ([f"cuda:{i} for i in range(1 if current_platform.device_count() == 1 else 2)"]
can refer to https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/37566 and https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/38901

3. implement lint check for string "cuda" and "cuda*", except tests/kernel, vllm/platforms, etc. 

### Limitation
This decorator can not work with the @create_new_process_for_each_test().
It is because vLLM's @create_new_process_for_each_test() forces the execution of the test function inside a completely separate, brand new OS subprocess to ensure CUDA runtime isolation, any process-specific Python state—including PyTorch’s active with torch.device(...) thread-local context wrapper—is completely erased when the new process boots up.

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

title: [Feature]: Prefix caching completely ineffective for Mamba-hybrid models (Qwen3.5) when prompt < block_size (528 tokens)
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

## Environment (Brief)

- vLLM version: 0.19.1
- GPU: NVIDIA A100/H20
- Model: Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B (Mamba-hybrid architecture)

## Description

When serving Mamba-hybrid models like Qwen3.5, vLLM sets the attention block size to **528 tokens** to align with the mamba page size:

```
INFO [config.py:281] Setting attention block size to 528 tokens to ensure that attention page size is >= mamba page size.
```

Since prefix caching operates at the **block** granularity, only **fully completed blocks** are cached. This means:

- Prompt with **< 528 tokens**: **0% prefix cache hit** — the entire prefix must be recomputed every request
- Prompt with 552 tokens: ~95% hit (1 block cached, only 24 tokens recomputed)
- Prompt with 979 tokens: ~54% hit (1 block cached, 451 tokens recomputed)

For comparison, standard transformer models use block_size=16, so even a 100-token prompt gets 6 fully cached blocks (96 tokens cached).

## Reproduction

```bash
# Start vllm serve with prefix caching
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --max-model-len 1024 \
  --dtype bfloat16

# Send requests with the same ~480 token prefix but different query suffixes
# Observe from vllm stats log:
# "Prefix cache hit rate: 0.0%"  (when total prompt < 528 tokens)
```

Measured results from our benchmark (200 requests each, same prefix, different short suffix):

| Prompt length | Full blocks | Prefix cache hit rate |
|---|---|---|
| 479 tokens | 0 | ~0% |
| 552 tokens | 1 | 95.4% |
| 597 tokens | 1 | 88.2% |
| 979 tokens | 1 | 53.7% |

## Impact

This is a severe performance cliff for **short-prompt, high-QPS workloads** common in production (classification, intent detection, routing, etc.). These tasks typically have prompts of 300-600 tokens. Users enabling `--enable-prefix-caching` expect it to help, but it silently does nothing — or even hurts performance due to the caching overhead.

In our case, QPS dropped from **200 to <100** when the prompt was shortened from ~560 to ~480 tokens, purely because it crossed below the 528-token block boundary.

## Suggested fix

For Mamba-hybrid models with large block sizes, consider one of:

1. **Sub-block prefix caching**: Allow caching at a finer granularity (e.g., 16-token chunks within the 528-token block), even if the mamba state requires full-block alignment for its own cache
2. **Automatic padding**: Pad the prefix to the next block boundary before caching, so that short prompts can still benefit
3. **Warn the user**: At minimum, log a warning when `enable_prefix_caching=True` and the block size is unusually large (>64), telling the user the minimum prompt length needed to benefit
4. **Decouple attention and mamba block sizes**: Use separate block sizes for the attention KV cache (small, e.g. 16) and the mamba state cache (large, 528), so prefix caching for attention layers is not penalized by mamba alignment requirements

Option 4 seems the most correct — there's no fundamental reason the attention KV cache block size needs to match the mamba page size for prefix caching purposes.


## Environment (Detail)：
```
==============================
        System Info
==============================
OS                           : Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS (x86_64)
GCC version                  : (Ubuntu 11.4.0-1ubuntu1~22.04.2) 11.4.0
Clang version                : Could not collect
CMake version                : version 4.1.0
Libc version                 : glibc-2.35

==============================
       PyTorch Info
==============================

Is debug build               : False
CUDA used to build PyTorch   : 12.8
ROCM used to build PyTorch   : N/A
XPU used to build PyTorch    : N/A

==============================

title: [BUG]  cu129 Nightly Installation Resolves to CUDA 13 Wheel
body:
## Description

The latest wheel available on the cu129 nightly channel is `0.20.2rc1.dev233+g5497ffbf7.cu129`, while PyPI now publishes `0.20.2` as the final release (built against CUDA 13). Per PEP 440, the cu129 pre-release version sorts below the PyPI stable release, causing the documented installation command to resolve to the PyPI artifact:

```bash
uv pip install -U vllm --pre \
  --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/nightly/cu129 \
  --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu129 \
  --index-strategy unsafe-best-match
```

This command installs `vllm 0.20.2`. Every compiled `.so` in the resulting installation links against `libcudart.so.13` (confirmed via `readelf -d`), causing CUDA 12 environments to fail at import with `ImportError: libcudart.so.13`.

Under a healthy release flow, cu129 nightlies should be versioned ahead of the stable release (for example, `0.20.3rc1.devN+cu129`) and would win resolution, allowing the documented command to behave as intended. The artifact catalog at `wheels.vllm.ai/nightly/cu129/` appears to be stalled.

title: [Bug]: DeepSeek V4 load_weights UnboundLocalError: 'name_mapped' when expert mapping has no match
body:
### Summary

`vllm/model_executor/models/deepseek_v4.py` has an unbound-local bug in `DeepseekV4ForCausalLM.load_weights()`'s expert branch. The variable `name_mapped` is assigned **inside** a `for mapping in expert_mapping` loop, but referenced **after** the loop. When no entry in `expert_mapping` matches the incoming tensor name (all iterations hit the early `continue`), `name_mapped` is never bound — but the subsequent `loaded_params.add(name_mapped)` still runs:

```
File "vllm/model_executor/models/deepseek_v4.py", line 1557, in load_weights
    loaded_params.add(name_mapped)
UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'name_mapped' where it is not associated with a value
```

### Environment

- vLLM: 0.21.0 (also reproducible on `main` as of 2026-05-15)
- Transformers: 4.57.1
- Hardware: 2× A100 80GB, TP=2
- Trigger: any DSV4 checkpoint whose expert weight tensor names don't match every entry in `get_expert_mapping()` (e.g., custom quantization-aware suffixes like `.tq_packed`).

### Affected code

`vllm/model_executor/models/deepseek_v4.py` around lines 1532-1558 (line numbers from main as of 2026-05-15, may drift slightly):

```python
                if ".experts." in name:
                    # E8M0 scales special handling...
                    if (
                        "weight_scale" in name
                        and loaded_weight.dtype == torch.float8_e8m0fnu
                    ):
                        loaded_weight = loaded_weight.view(torch.uint8)
                    for mapping in expert_mapping:
                        param_name, weight_name, expert_id, shard_id = mapping
                        if weight_name not in name:
                            continue                 # <-- early continue
                        name_mapped = name.replace(weight_name, param_name)
                        # ... weight loader call ...
                        if success:
                            name = name_mapped
                            break
                    loaded_params.add(name_mapped)   # <-- unbound if loop never set it
                    continue
```

If every iteration `continue`s on the `if weight_name not in name` guard, the `for` loop exits without `break` AND without ever assigning `name_mapped`. `loaded_params.add(name_mapped)` then raises `UnboundLocalError`.

### Repro

Easiest path: load any DSV4 checkpoint that includes an expert tensor name not present in `get_expert_mapping()`'s output. We hit it loading a TQ3-native variant where weight names have a `.tq_packed` suffix, but it would also fire on:
- Custom quantization schemes that decorate weight names
- Any checkpoint shape mismatch where `.experts.` is in the name but the suffix doesn't match the expected `gate_proj`/`up_proj`/`down_proj`/`w1`/`w2`/`w3` patterns

### Proposed fix

Initialize `name_mapped = None` before the loop, then short-circuit if it stayed unset:

```python
                if ".experts." in name:
                    if (
                        "weight_scale" in name
                        and loaded_weight.dtype == torch.float8_e8m0fnu
                    ):
                        loaded_weight = loaded_weight.view(torch.uint8)
                    name_mapped = None               # <-- ADDED
                    for mapping in expert_mapping:
                        param_name, weight_name, expert_id, shard_id = mapping
                        if weight_name not in name:
                            continue
                        name_mapped = name.replace(weight_name, param_name)
                        # ... weight loader call ...
                        if success:
                            name = name_mapped
                            break
                    if name_mapped is None:          # <-- ADDED
                        continue                     # <-- ADDED
                    loaded_params.add(name_mapped)
                    continue
```

Three-line change. Skips unrecognized expert tensors cleanly instead of raising. If a maintainer prefers raising explicitly for unrecognized expert names, the `continue` could be `raise ValueError(f"unrecognized expert tensor name: {name}")` — that's a stylistic choice.

### Workaround we're using

Patching the installed `deepseek_v4.py` at runtime via a setup script (`sed`-style replace with the diff above). Three-line surgical patch.

### Context

We've been validating a TQ3-native (3-bit weight quantization) version of DeepSeek-V4-Flash on vLLM. This is the second `deepseek_v4.py` bug we've hit during that work; the first was reported as [#42741](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/42741) (`compress_ratios` attribute access vs the new transformers normalization). Happy to submit a PR with both fixes together if a maintainer wants.

---

title: [Feature]: IndexCache support for DeepSeek V4
body:
### Summary

Extend the existing IndexCache feature (currently only supported for DeepSeek-V3.2 / GLM-5 DSA models) to DeepSeek V4's c4a attention layers, which also use DSA lightning indexer with top-k token selection.

### Motivation

DeepSeek V4 uses a hybrid compressed attention architecture with two layer types:

- **c4a layers** (30 layers): Compressed KV + **DSA lightning indexer** (top-k=1024) + sparse attention
- **c128a layers** (31 layers): Heavily compressed KV, near-full attention (no indexer needed)
- **SWA layer** (1 layer): Pure sliding window, no indexer

The 30 c4a layers have the same DSA lightning indexer as V3.2, making them **directly amenable to IndexCache optimization** — skipping redundant top-k computation across layers by reusing cached `topk_indices`.

This is not theoretical — **vllm-ascend has already implemented and validated it**:


### Existing Implementation & Validation

**vllm-ascend PR**: [[Feature] IndexCache: reuse topk_indices across decode steps for DSA models (DeepSeek V4)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/pull/9390) — **Merged** on 2026-05-25

**Performance (DeepSeek V4-Flash, Ascend 910B4, 32K input / 1K output)**:

| Metric | Baseline | IndexCache (freq=4) | Improvement |
|--------|----------|---------------------|-------------|
| Throughput (tok/s) | 1,423 | 1,554 | **+9.18%** |
| TTFT (ms) | 6,182 | 5,813 | **-5.97%** |
| TPOT (ms) | 186.4 | 171.8 | **-7.83%** |

**Accuracy (GPQA-diamond)**: −0.51 pt (within acceptable range)

### Technical Feasibility

The V4 model config confirms c4a layers have full DSA indexer support:

```json
// DeepSeek-V4-Pro config.json
{
  "index_topk": 1024,
  "index_n_heads": 64,
  "index_head_dim": 128,
  "compress_ratios": [128, 128, 4, 128, 4, 128, 4, ...]  // 30 layers with ratio=4 (c4a)
}
```

Key observations from the vLLM v0.22.0 codebase:

1. **V3.2 IndexCache is already implemented** in `deepseek_v2.py` (lines ~1009-1019), using `use_index_cache` / `index_topk_freq` / `index_topk_pattern` config fields
2. **V4's `DeepseekV4Indexer`** already uses `topk_indices_buffer` (shared across layers) — the buffer infrastructure is in place
3. **V4's `SparseAttnIndexer`** already writes `topk_indices_buffer` in both prefill and decode paths
4. **V4's `DeepseekV4MLAWrapper.forward`** already has the `if self.indexer is not None` check — the hook point for `skip_topk` is natural

**What's missing** (roughly ~65 lines of code):

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `deepseek_v4/nvidia/model.py` | Read `use_index_cache` config, compute `skip_topk` per layer, pass to MLA modules (~20 lines) |
| `deepseek_v4/amd/model.py` | Same as above for AMD path (~20 lines) |
| `deepseek_v4/attention.py` | Add `skip_topk` to `DeepseekV4MLAModules` dataclass + conditional skip in `DeepseekV4MLAWrapper.forward` (~15 lines) |
| Tests | E2E test for V4 with `use_index_cache=True` (~50 lines) |

### Layer Index Mapping

V4 has heterogeneous layer types — `index_topk_pattern` should map to the **sequence of c4a layers only** (not all 62 layers), consistent with vllm-ascend's approach:

```python
# From vllm-ascend PR #9390
indexer_seq_idx = sum(1 for r in compress_ratios[:layer_idx] if r == 4)
if pattern is None:
    skip_topk = max(indexer_seq_idx - 1, 0) % freq != 0
else:
    skip_topk = pattern[indexer_seq_idx] == "S"
```

For V4-Pro (30 c4a layers), `index_topk_freq=4` would keep ~8 F-layers and skip ~22 S-layers.

### Proposed API

Consistent with existing V3.2 IndexCache:

```bash
# Using index_topk_freq (uniform)
vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro \
  --hf-overrides '{"use_index_cache": true, "index_topk_freq": 4}'

# Using index_topk_pattern (custom, for c4a layers only)
vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro \
  --hf-overrides '{"use_index_cache": true, "index_topk_pattern": "FFSFSSSFSSFFF..."}'
```

### References

- **IndexCache paper**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.12201
- **vLLM V3.2 IndexCache PR**: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/37735
- **vLLM V3.2 IndexCache MTP share PR**: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/44420
- **vllm-ascend V4 IndexCache PR**: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/pull/9390
- **SGLang IndexCache PR (V3.2)**: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/21405
- **THUDM/IndexCache reference implementation**: https://github.com/THUDM/IndexCache

title: [Bug]: finish_reason is "tool_calls" for a turn truncated at max_tokens, hiding the length stop from clients
body:
**Environment.** As in A.

**Describe the bug.** When a generation is cut off by `max_tokens` but any tool call was parsed, the response reports `finish_reason: "tool_calls"` rather than `"length"`. In `vllm/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/serving.py` the finish reason is computed as `auto_tools_called or (tool_choice == "required" and output.finish_reason == "stop")`, and `auto_tools_called` wins regardless of why generation stopped.

**Impact.** A client cannot tell a completed tool-calling turn from one guillotined mid-argument. Agent harnesses use `finish_reason` to decide whether to continue, retry with a larger budget, or execute; here they execute a call that may be the last complete one before the cut. It also silently corrupts any analysis that filters on the finish reason.

**Frequency.** 25 of 3,600 generations in our suite hit the cap exactly; each reported `tool_calls`. They were identifiable only by comparing `usage.completion_tokens` with the request's `max_tokens`.

**Suggested fix.** Let `length` win over the tool-call relabel, or surface the underlying stop reason alongside it.

AI assistance was used for the investigation and the measurement harness; I reviewed the findings and ran everything described here on my own hardware.

title: [Bug]: an unclosed <tool_call> opener written in prose holds the Qwen3 parser in tool state and swallows a later genuine tool call
body:
**Environment.** As in A (Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4, vLLM 0.28.0, `qwen3_coder`, template sha256 `0a20a467…abab9ab`).

**Describe the bug.** When the model mentions `<tool_call>` in prose without closing it — common when it explains or demonstrates the tool-call format — the state machine stays in tool state. Everything after is consumed as that span's body, including `</think>` and including a subsequent genuine tool call, which is therefore never emitted. The client receives a call named after the *first*, quoted block and does not receive the real one.

**Frequency.** 131 of 3,600 generations (3.6%) in our suite contain unbalanced `<tool_call>` markup (openers ≠ closers); 119 of those come from a prompt that asks the model to show the markup. At least one loses a genuine call as described.

**Concrete instance.** One generation, character offsets into the decoded output:

```
 2470  <tool_call>            <- opener, never closed
 2482  <function=function_name
 2890  <tool_call>            <- second opener, never closed
 4493  </think>
 4503  <tool_call>
 4515  <function=get_weather  <- the genuine call
 4586  </tool_call>           <- closes the span opened at 2470
```

The server returned `['function_name', 'get_weather', 'function_name']`; the final `function_name` is the span opened at 2,470 and closed at 4,586, and the real `get_weather` at 4,503 is inside its body. Replaying this through `Qwen3Parser` reproduces it exactly.

**Why the adjacent work does not cover it.** #56658 / #56661 add a function-header check before committing a span; this span *has* a header (`<function=function_name`), so that check confirms it rather than rejecting it. #50986 (`validate_tool_names`) drops the outer span because `function_name` is not offered — but the genuine call is inside that span's body and is dropped with it. Neither recovers the lost call.

**Suggested direction.** Bound how far a tool span may run — a turn-boundary or `</think>` token inside an open span is strong evidence the opener was prose, not markup — or reconsider the span at `finish()` when it never closed lexically. Raw generations available.

AI assistance was used for the investigation and the measurement harness; I reviewed the findings and ran everything described here on my own hardware.

title: [Performance][ROCm]: Narrower KV tiles speed up Triton embedding/reranking attention on RDNA3/RDNA4
body:
### Proposal to improve performance ## Problem `context_attention_fwd` in `vllm/v1/attention/ops/triton_prefill_attention.py` launches `_fwd_kernel` with a square tile: ```python BLOCK = get_block_size(q.dtype) # 128 for bf16/fp16 ... BLOCK_M=BLOCK, BLOCK_N=BLOCK, ``` That is one tile shape for every backend. It is a reasonable default on CDNA, but RDNA3/RDNA4 are wave32 with a much smaller LDS budget, which makes a 128-wide KV tile a poor fit. I have not profiled the stall reason, so treat the mechanism as a hypothesis; what is measured is that the narrower tile is faster everywhere I tested. There is currently no ROCm- or RDNA-specific handling anywhere in this kernel. ## Who is affected This kernel is reached through `EncoderOnlyAttention` and non-causal pooling in the `TRITON_ATTN` and `ROCM_ATTN` backends, so the affected workloads are **embedding and reranking models on RDNA3 and RDNA4**. Generation prefill and decode use separate attention paths and are unaffected by this change. Call-count instrumentation records zero calls into this kernel for the generation model tested. `vit_attn_wrappers.py` can reach this kernel as well, but on RDNA it does not: `RocmPlatform.get_vit_attn_backend()` returns `FLASH_ATTN` when `on_gfx1x()` and otherwise falls back to `TORCH_SDPA`, so ViT is only affected if the backend is set explicitly. ## Size of the prize Narrowing **only** the KV tile to 32, leaving `BLOCK_M`, `num_warps` and `num_stages` at their current values, measured on W7900 (gfx1100) and R9700 (gfx1201), bf16, TP=1, at stock clocks: | | gfx1100 | gfx1201 | | --- | --- | --- | | kernel, median of 36 cells | **2.56x-2.67x** | **2.25x-2.30x** | | offline end-to-end embedding latency | **1.10x-1.23x** | 1.08x-1.12x | | serving throughput (`vllm bench serve`) | **1.17x-1.19x** | 1.03x-1.05x | The kernel figure covers all 9 head sizes in `get_supported_head_sizes()` crossed with all four mask modes the kernel exposes, at batch 4, sequence 2048, 12 query heads and 2 KV heads. The median is a range because the matrix was run four times per architecture (two devices, two sessions) and the median moves more between runs than the cells it summarises do — on the same four runs and the same measure, 4.3% against 2.1% for the typical cell on gfx1100. So the claim to rely on is not the median: **all 36 cells are faster than the current launch in all four runs on both architectures** — 288 of 288 cell measurements, the slowest anywhere being 1.08x. None regresses. Both arms launch the installed kernel module itself, so the windowed modes include the sliding-window loop-range trim. Offline end-to-end speedups measure `LLM.embed()` on repeated synthetic text, with eager execution and prefix caching disabled. Each value is the median stock/tuned latency ratio across 24 interleaved pairs in one process (ABBA ordering), under the bf16, TP=1, stock-clock conditions above: | Model | Batch | Approx. tokens per sequence | gfx1100 | gfx1201 | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Alibaba-NLP/gte-Qwen2-1.5B-instruct | 8 | 2048 | **1.226x** | **1.083x** | | BAAI/bge-base-en | 32 | 500 | **1.100x** | **1.118x** | | unsloth/gemma-3-1b-it (forced non-causal) | 8 | 2048 | **1.107x** | **1.123x** | Five of those six are unanimous, 24 of 24 pairs favouring the narrower tile. bge on gfx1100 is the exception at 21 of 24, and also has the widest bootstrap interval, [1.086, 1.115]. gemma on gfx1201 is the next loosest at [1.114, 1.135]; the remaining four intervals are all under 0.008 wide. Two of the three models measured reach this kernel as shipped: `Alibaba-NLP/gte-Qwen2-1.5B-instruct`, whose config already sets `is_causal: false`, and `BAAI/bge-base-en`, which is encoder-only. The third does not. `--convert embed` changes pooling but not attention type, and `gemma3.py` reads `getattr(config, "is_causal", True)`, so `unsloth/gemma-3-1b-it` takes the decoder path unless it is forced: ``` --convert embed --hf-overrides '{"is_causal": false}' ``` That is a constructed configuration, included because it is the only head_dim 256 case I had, not a deployment anyone is running today. The serving figures use gte-Qwen2 alone: ``` vllm serve Alibaba-NLP/gte-Qwen2-1.5B-instruct \ --runner pooling --max-model-len 4096 --enforce-eager vllm bench serve --backend openai-embeddings --endpoint /v1/embeddings \ --model Alibaba-NLP/gte-Qwen2-1.5B-instruct \ --dataset-name random --random-input-len 2048 --random-output-len 1 \ --num-prompts 200 --max-concurrency C --num-warmups C ``` at concurrency 1/4/16/64. The `--backend` and `--endpoint` flags matter: they default to `openai` and `/v1/completions`, which would not exercise this path at all. gfx1201 gains less end to end than gfx1100 while its baseline is also the faster one (14.7 against 9.85 req/s). This evidence does not break request time down by stage, so why the end-to-end gain is smaller there is not established. At the kernel level the two architectures agree closely, which is why one predicate should cover both. ## Flagged up front - **Not measured:** fp16, TP>1, and RDNA parts other than gfx1100/gfx1201. float32 is provably unaffected, since `get_block_size` already returns 32 for it. - **Weakest case end to end:** small rerankers. `ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2` does route here and the kernel is **1.598x** faster at the bidirectional mode a cross-encoder uses. Multiplying isolated kernel latency by its 6 layers gives an estimated attention share of 6.1% (6 x 0.471ms of 46.59ms), predicting a 2.3% request-time saving if other costs stay unchanged; measured end to end is **1.016x**. `bge-reranker-base` (12 layers, hidden 768, head_dim 64) has an estimated share of 16.8% by the same calculation and gains **1.0955x** end to end on gfx1100, with 24 of 24 pairs favouring the narrower tile, close to the embedding results on the same device. These results are consistent with an attention-share explanation, but the shares are estimates, not in-request profiles. Only gfx1100 was measured for rerankers. - **Weakest kernel case:** head_dim 32 on gfx1201, 1.42x median and 1.08x in its weakest mask mode (`encoder`) — which is also the slowest cell anywhere, and still a gain in every mask mode. - **Accuracy:** SciFact. Four model/architecture pairs exercise the proposal: | Model | Arch | baseline nDCG@10 | dnDCG@10 | drecall@10 | | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | gte-Qwen2-1.5B-instruct | gfx1100 | 0.7857 | -0.00014 | 0 | | gte-Qwen2-1.5B-instruct | gfx1201 | 0.7853 | -0.00051 | 0 | | bge-base-en | gfx1201 | 0.6033 | +0.00081 | +0.00333 | | gemma-3-1b-it | gfx1201 | 0.0496 | -0.00065 | -0.00333 | recall@10 is unchanged for both gte pairs and moves by exactly +-1/300 of the macro average for bge and for gemma, in opposite directions. Since recall is averaged per query over 300 queries, that is consistent with one single-relevant query flipping, but equally with two two-relevant queries each moving by half, and only aggregate metrics were stored, so I cannot tell which. For GTE, unchanged re-runs reproduce the baseline metrics bit for bit on both architectures. Equivalent repeat controls were not collected for bge or gemma, so their changes cannot be conclusively attributed to accumulation order. The gemma row needs reading with care. Forced non-causal, it barely retrieves at all — nDCG 0.0496 and recall 0.0762, against 0.786 and 0.931 for gte — so the same 0.00333 that is a 0.46% relative move for bge is a 4.4% one there. It is weak evidence either way. For scale, a control that changes `max_num_seqs` alone, reordering bf16 accumulation without touching any kernel, moves nDCG@10 by 0.00113 on gte/gfx1100 where the patch moves 0.00014, and by 0.00157 on gemma where the patch moves 0.00065. On gte/gfx1201 the two are the same size, 0.00049 against 0.00051, and bge — which has the largest patch move of the four — has no control run at all. So where a control exists the two are of comparable magnitude, and on gte/gfx1201 the patch is fractionally the larger of the two. One control run per pair gives a sense of scale; it is not an error bound and not a proof of harmlessness. **bge-base-en on gfx1100 is not in the table**: it was run under an earlier `Lk >= 80` gate that excluded its head_dim 64, making it a no-op control rather than a test of this proposal. gemma-3-1b-it was not run on gfx1100, and its row is the forced non-causal configuration described above rather than a stock one. - The kernel matrix is replicated on two devices per architecture and the medians agree to 0.11% (gfx1100) and 1.1% (gfx1201). The end-to-end and serving numbers come from one device per architecture and are not replicated. ## Proposed direction A `min(BLOCK, 32)` override on `BLOCK_N` only, behind the existing `vllm.platforms.rocm.on_gfx1x()` predicate — which already excludes gfx10xx and the CDNA-classified gfx1250. No new configuration surface, no per-architecture table and no head-size gate: gfx1100 and gfx1201 prefer the same tile at every head size measured. A 96-configuration sweep over (`BLOCK_M`, `BLOCK_N`) x `num_warps` x `num_stages` found no tuple that beats it consistently. (That sweep ran on the pre-correction snapshot and covers the `encoder` mask mode only. On those cells the two kernel sources agree to 0.58% median per cell on gfx1100 and 0.55% on gfx1201, but the worst cell differs by 9.3%, so treat it as indicative of the ranking rather than conclusive; it has not been re-run on the upstream kernel.) The existing `num_warps = 4 if Lk <= 64 else 8` rule, with the narrowed tile, is the fastest of the four configurations carried through the full matrix in 47 of the 72 cells across the two architectures, so it is left alone. title: [Feature]: mega-MoE expert path for SM90 (H100/H20) DeepSeek-V4 / V4.1-Flash — Marlin weight-only is the only option today
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

A mega-MoE expert path for SM90 (H100/H20) DeepSeek-V4 / V4.1-Flash.

The RFC #42284 mega-MoE work landed, but both new paths are gated away from Hopper, so DeepSeek-V4/V4.1 on SM90 still falls back to weight-only Marlin — which dequantizes MXFP4 to bf16 and leaves the fp8 tensor cores idle. A SM90 mega-MoE (fp8-only) variant would directly address the main throughput bottleneck on the most common Hopper serving fleet.

What is gated away on SM90:

- `deep_gemm_mega_moe` (native): `DeepGEMM MegaMoE requires SM100 GPUs` (`vllm/models/deepseek_v4/nvidia/model.py`, `DeepseekV4MegaMoEExperts`) — the kernel consumes fp4 tensor cores.
- `flashinfer_moe_ep_mega_*`: requires an NVFP4-quantized checkpoint (fp8-e4m3 per-16 block scales + per-tensor `weight_scale_2`); MXFP4 checkpoints are rejected with "deep_gemm consumes the MXFP4 checkpoint instead".

So on SM90 there is no fused/quantized-MMA MoE option at all for the V4 family: only the weight-only Marlin/MXFP4 fixed-block kernel.

### Alternatives

1. An SM90 mega-MoE variant (fp8 weights/MMA, no fp4 tensor cores — e.g. via DeepGEMM fp8 grouped GEMM with the same fused dispatch→Linear1→Act→Linear2→combine structure).
2. Extending the flashinfer moe_ep path to accept MXFP4 checkpoints on Hopper.
3. Status quo: stay on Marlin. Config-level tuning is a dead end — `VLLM_TUNED_CONFIG_FOLDER` triton MoE configs are ineffective for this model (it does not go through the triton fused_moe path), so Marlin is the ceiling unless a new kernel path exists.

### Additional context

Measured on 8×H20 (TP8, MXFP4 checkpoint, zero offload): conc64 / mt=256 **2434 tok/s**; conc256 short-output **~3300 tok/s**; 128K cold prefill 17.3 s (0 errors, unique-marker bench). DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is 510 GB / 48 shards; 8×H20 fits it entirely in VRAM, so the fleet this targets is exactly Hopper.

Happy to benchmark any WIP branch on 8×H20 and share numbers.

title: [Bug] NIXL lease reaper strands expired KV blocks behind a heartbeated head entry
body:
### Your current environment

`v0.27.1`. Found by source inspection; the repro below is standalone stdlib and
needs no vLLM install. I have not yet quantified the runtime impact on a live
deployment — filing this because the control flow looks unambiguous and the
reclaim path it affects is shared by both NIXL connector modes.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

The NIXL lease reaper in `NixlConnectorWorker` relies on `_reqs_to_send` being ordered by expiry, but `_handle_heartbeat` breaks that invariant. A request that keeps receiving heartbeats can sit at the head of the dict and block every entry behind it from ever being reaped, even long after those entries' leases expire.

**The invariant.** The reaper exits at the first non-expired entry:

```python
# vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/base_worker.py (~L2147)
while self._reqs_to_send:
    req_id, expires = next(iter(self._reqs_to_send.items()))
    # Sorted dict, oldest requests are put first so we can exit early.
    if now < expires:
        break
    ...
    del self._reqs_to_send[req_id]
```

That is correct only while expiry order matches insertion order.

**What breaks it.** Heartbeats update the value in place:

```python
# same file (~L2198)
if req_id in self._reqs_to_send:
    old = self._reqs_to_send[req_id]
    self._reqs_to_send[req_id] = max(old, new_expiry)
```

Updating an existing key in a Python `dict` does not change its insertion position, so a renewed request keeps its original (early) slot while its expiry moves arbitrarily far into the future. Requests are inserted once (`pull_worker.py` asserts `req_id not in self._reqs_to_send` before inserting), so the position is never revisited.

**Consequence.** This is the common case under load: the oldest pending-send request is the one most likely to still be queued on D, and therefore the one being heartbeated, while newer requests behind it are not.

### Minimal reproduction

```python
LEASE_DURATION = 30.0     # kv_lease_duration default
LEASE_EXTENSION = 20.0    # kv_lease_duration * 2 // 3

def reap(reqs_to_send, now):                      # verbatim control flow
    done = []
    while reqs_to_send:
        req_id, expires = next(iter(reqs_to_send.items()))
        if now < expires:
            break
        del reqs_to_send[req_id]
        done.append(req_id)
    return done

def handle_heartbeat(reqs_to_send, req_id, now):  # verbatim
    if req_id in reqs_to_send:
        reqs_to_send[req_id] = max(reqs_to_send[req_id], now + LEASE_EXTENSION)

reqs = {"A": 0.0 + LEASE_DURATION,   # 30.0, enters first, stays queued on D
        "B": 2.0 + LEASE_DURATION,   # 32.0, never renewed
        "C": 4.0 + LEASE_DURATION}   # 34.0, never renewed
for t in (20.0, 40.0, 60.0, 80.0):
    handle_heartbeat(reqs, "A", t)   # A -> 100.0, still at the head

for now in (35.0, 50.0, 90.0):
    print(now, reap(dict(reqs), now))
```

Output:

```
35.0 []
50.0 []
90.0 []
```

`B` and `C` expired at `t=32.0` and `t=34.0`. At `t=90.0` neither has been released. They stay stranded for as long as `A` keeps receiving heartbeats, which by design can be indefinite ("each heartbeat extends the lease ... keeping blocks alive indefinitely while D is healthy" — `docs/design/nixl_kv_cache_lease.md`).

### Impact

Blocks that should have been reclaimed within `kv_lease_duration` (default 30s) of their reader disconnecting are held indefinitely on P, reducing available KV cache. This is the exact failure mode lease renewal was introduced to avoid (#41383): the design doc motivates the short initial lease by noting that under the old fixed 480s timeout "P would hold onto potentially several GBs of 'dead' blocks for up to 8 minutes". The head-of-line case restores that behaviour without a bound.

It also makes `vllm:nixl_num_kv_expired_reqs` under-report, since stranded entries are never passed to `record_kv_expired_req()`.

### Note on one fix that does *not* work

Re-inserting on heartbeat (delete + insert to move the entry to the tail) does not restore the invariant, because `max(old, now + extension)` can still be smaller than a later-inserted entry's initial expiry:

```
Y inserted t=0   -> expiry 30
X inserted t=25  -> expiry 55
Y renewed at t=26 -> max(30, 46) = 46, moved to tail
order: X(55), Y(46)   # at now=50, X blocks the already-expired Y
```

### Candidate fixes

1. **Scan all entries** instead of exiting early. Simplest and obviously correct; `O(n)` per step in the number of pending sends rather than amortized `O(1)`.
2. **Expiry-ordered heap with lazy deletion.** Push `(expiry, req_id)` on insert and on each renewal; pop while `top.expiry <= now` and skip entries whose expiry no longer matches the dict. `O(log n)`, more code.
3. **Keep the dict, maintain a separate ordered index** keyed by expiry.

Happy to send a PR for whichever shape maintainers prefer.

One thing to check alongside the fix: the reaper calls `self._reqs_to_process.remove(req_id)` (`base_worker.py` ~L2160) while other paths use `.discard()` (`pull_worker.py` ~L90). Any fix that reaps entries the current code never reaches will exercise that line for request IDs it previously never saw, so `remove()` vs `discard()` there may need a second look.

### Related but distinct

- #53095 (`NixlPushConnector heartbeat fails to renew KV leases`) is the opposite
  direction: leases expiring while the consumer still wants the blocks. This
  report is about a renewed entry preventing *other* entries from expiring. Both
  touch `_handle_heartbeat` / `_reqs_to_send` in `base_worker.py`, which is shared
  by the push and pull paths, so a fix here may be worth checking against that
  report.
- #46283 concerns decode-side *recv* blocks leaking on abort, and notes in passing
  that the `_reqs_to_send` reaper covers only the send side. That observation is
  consistent with this report but the defect is a different one.
- #53128 (closed) is the `TieringOffloadingSpec` p2p `_UNBOUND_STORE_TIMEOUT_S`
  path, a separate mechanism.

title: [RFC]: Per-instance EPLB metrics
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

(co-authored with @sallyom and Claude)

In replicated vLLM deployments behind a load balancer, the load balancer has no visibility into EPLB (Expert-Parallel Load Balancing) state when making routing decisions. EPLB dynamically replicates heavily-used experts across EP ranks to balance load, and instances experiencing high expert load imbalance or active rebalancing operations have degraded capacity. Without metrics exposing this state, load balancers cannot avoid routing traffic to struggling instances, leading to suboptimal performance and increased tail latencies.

EPLB already tracks and logs this information to stdout when `--eplb-log-balancedness` is enabled:

```
EPLB step: 2500: avg_tokens=1024, max_tokens=2048, balancedness=0.5000
```

But these are obviously not queryable by load balancers. This proposal exports the same data that's currently logged as Prometheus metrics, enabling intelligent load balancing decisions based on instance health.

Note - these stats are EP-group-wide, and should not be reported per-engine (i.e. with the `engine_idx` label), instead they should probably only be recorded on DP rank 0.

## Proposed Metrics

| Metric Name | Type | Description
|-------------|------|-------------|
| `vllm:eplb_avg_tokens_per_rank` | Gauge | Average tokens per EP rank in current interval |
| `vllm:eplb_max_tokens_per_rank` | Gauge | Maximum tokens across EP ranks in current interval |
| `vllm:eplb_rebalancing` | Gauge | Whether EPLB is currently rebalancing (0 or 1) |
| `vllm:eplb_rebalance_events_total` | Counter | Total number of EPLB rebalancing operations |

## Sample PromQL

```promql
# Imbalance ratio - 0.5 means 50% balanced
(vllm:eplb_avg_tokens_per_rank / vllm:eplb_max_tokens_per_rank)

# Relative imbalance: avoid instances where one rank is 2x overloaded
(vllm:eplb_max_tokens_per_rank / vllm:eplb_avg_tokens_per_rank) > 2.0

# Absolute imbalance: avoid instances with severe token gap
(vllm:eplb_max_tokens_per_rank - vllm:eplb_avg_tokens_per_rank) > 5000

# Hybrid: high load AND poor balance (most dangerous)
vllm:eplb_max_tokens_per_rank > 15000
AND (vllm:eplb_max_tokens_per_rank / vllm:eplb_avg_tokens_per_rank) > 1.5

# Alert on thrashing
rate(vllm:eplb_rebalance_events_total[5m]) > 2

# Reduce traffic to instance currently rebalancing
vllm:eplb_rebalancing == 1
```

### Alternatives

_No response_

_No response_

title: [Roadmap] vLLM Roadmap Q3 2026
body:
In [#32455](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/32455), we broke down vLLM's goal into various special interest groups (SIGs). Please find below each SIG's Q3 roadmap. You can find regular meetings of these SIGs on the public vLLM calendar.

## Key takeaway

* **Agentic Workload:** In Q2, vLLM doubled down on core performance reaching TensorRT-level speed-of-light performance for top models, along with production features such as disaggregated serving and KV offloading maturity. In Q3, we focus on production agentic workload and high-interactivity premium tokens.
* **Ecosystem:** The ecosystem has been stronger than ever: quantization (`ModelOpt` and `llm-compressor`), speculations (`Speculators` and `TorchSpec`), and RL (`vime`, `Prime-RL`, `Nemo-RL`, etc.) are three established main ecosystems surrounding core vLLM. vLLM-Omni has reached maturity with a flywheel of model + hardware + optimization support.
* **OSS Maintenance:** The rise of coding agents brought new challenges to open source maintenance. We are re-engineering vLLM core abstractions (`Flat Model`), developer infrastructure (`nightly model quality test`), security processes (`CVE and disclosure`), and model / hardware / features lifecycle management: when to add, who to contact, and when to remove.
